sources.title: How Justin Welsh builds a one-person business: LinkedIn attention, service-to-product, impulse-buy pricing
sources.originalTitle: Justin Welsh Shows You How To Start & Grow A One-Person Business
sources.summary: Justin Welsh explains how he went from burned-out SaaS executive to a one-person business by writing daily on LinkedIn and turning that attention into low-priced products and a community. He covers his post structure, pricing, and why he starts with a service business before productizing.

principles.text: Stand out by using a platform differently than everyone else on it; LinkedIn used like Twitter was an edge.
principles.quote: I'm going to go use LinkedIn just like people use Twitter. Because nobody else was doing that, I stood out.

principles.text: Get early traction by commenting first, with real value, under posts from a few big creators in your space.
principles.quote: And whenever they post in the morning or in the afternoon or whatever, get there first. But get there first with value.

principles.text: Price products as impulse buys that act as trust tripwires, and rely on organic audience over paid ads.
principles.quote: Most of my stuff is what I call trust tripwires, right? So, it's getting people in with a lower cost product that delivers incredible value

principles.text: Customers pay for aggregation and speed, not secrets, so share everything free and sell the packaged version.
principles.quote: People don't pay me for some new secret, even though they believe they are.

principles.text: Start with a service business for people you like helping, then productize what works across clients.
principles.quote: I'm a big fan of service before product and because I think you learn so much for your product by first having a service business.

principles.text: One-person businesses are mostly marketing; solving the problem is only part of it, attention is the rest.
principles.quote: to me, one-person businesses are mostly about marketing.

sources.title: How Justin Welsh built a $5M one-person business: life first, solve problems, play the long game
sources.originalTitle: How To Start A $5,000,000 Business With Zero Stress | Justin Welsh
sources.summary: Justin Welsh explains how burnout led him to build a one-person business that hit $5M. He covers starting fast on one platform, turning audience questions into products, de-risking with diversified revenue, discovery-based selling, pricing courses low for trust, and building a movement.

principles.text: Design your life first and the business second; build a business that supports the life you want.
principles.quote: your life should come first your business should come second if you build your life that way and you build a business that supports your life you build in free time you build in breaks

principles.text: Start before you feel ready; pick a platform you will actually use daily, since consistency beats perfect planning.
principles.quote: start then learn don't learn then start just get started and watch how the journey unfolds

principles.text: Make your first dollar by teaching publicly, then listen to audience questions and solve the common problems you hear.
principles.quote: look around see what's happening see what people are asking you there's gold there

principles.text: Presell before building: gather demand signals, offer a presale, and only build if enough people pay.
principles.quote: don't build something unless people want to pay for it

principles.text: Price courses low and over-deliver to earn trust and testimonials, which compound conversions and word of mouth.
principles.quote: I would rather someone paid $150 and got 15 grand worth of value or 150 Grand worth of value

principles.text: De-risk with layered revenue: a service, a product, sponsorships, and cheap subscriptions under one audience.
principles.quote: it's a $27,000 a month business where I send one email so now you've got a service business a product business sponsorships subscription email

sources.title: How Justin Welsh built a one-person business: validate cheap, talk to customers, grow slow
sources.originalTitle: How to Build a One-Person Business in 2025 | Justin Welsh
sources.summary: Justin Welsh explains how he moved from SaaS advising to a solopreneur course and newsletter business. He covers quitting gradually, using customer feedback to choose products, pricing and positioning, and why slow, trust-based growth beats hacks. He also shares how he uses AI as a sounding board rather than a writer.

principles.text: Get a side income to roughly 60-70% of your salary before quitting; scaling from there is far likelier than starting at zero.
principles.quote: if you can get to 60 65 70% of your current take-home earnings doing your side job

principles.text: Beginners need specific, tactical how-to steps, not inspiration or high-level strategy.
principles.quote: they don't need inspiration they don't need pie in the sky strategy they don't need 30,000 foot view they need like how do I do this thing

principles.text: Start with a cheap product because selling expensive offers requires audience trust you haven't built yet; then grow the price and audience over time.
principles.quote: I don't think people recognize the amount of trust that you have to build in order to sell something really expensive

principles.text: A service business is the easiest way to get paid while talking to future customers and collecting product feedback.
principles.quote: the service business is essentially you're getting paid to talk to people

principles.text: Pivot only when the same request shows up repeatedly from the same prospect type, not on a one-off idea.
principles.quote: what I want to see is the same question 25 50 75 100 times coming from the same sort of Prospect

principles.text: Diversify revenue under one thesis, and add products only to fill gaps customers tell you about.
principles.quote: it's listening to the customers recognizing a gap in what they want to know and then figuring out a new way to solve that Gap

sources.title: Justin Welsh on running a ~$15M one-person business and what to sell in the AI era
sources.originalTitle: Justin Welsh: How I Built A $15M Business Alone l Trailblazers Podcast Episode 38
sources.summary: Justin Welsh breaks down his revenue mix (courses, newsletter sponsorships, partnerships, membership), how AI commoditization forced him to rethink his model, and why he's betting on authentic writing and proximity. He also covers choosing a medium, using AI as an editor, storytelling over how-tos, and bootstrapping.

principles.text: Pick the medium you love and get excellent at it; the best channel is that medium, not a platform.
principles.quote: the most valuable channel is whatever medium you become excellent at. So there are only so many mediums. There's video, there's audio, there's writing.

principles.text: Don't use a platform you dislike just because it has reach; try mediums and keep the one you enjoy.
principles.quote: going on a platform and doing something you dislike simply because it has reach the definition of a bad life to me.

principles.text: As AI commoditizes information and products, monetize proximity and authentic writing instead.
principles.quote: One one thing that you can sell is you can lean heavily into AI. It's just not me.

principles.text: Use AI as an editor and thought partner after writing yourself, so you keep your own writing skill.
principles.quote: I can write my stuff and then I can push it through an AI and say like where are the gaps?

principles.text: Distribution is an accelerant, not a must-have; tell a unique story and be someone people want to follow.
principles.quote: I think it's an accelerant, not a must-have.

principles.text: Prefer bootstrapping and compounding small wins over big moonshots; keep margins high and ask how much you need.
principles.quote: I'd rather have 10 wins and have two of them eventually not be wins and have eight wins left over than take a moonshot and be left with nothing.

sources.title: How Justin Welsh built an $8M solo business: niche down, validate 1:1, run a simple funnel
sources.originalTitle: How I Built an $8M Business with 0 Employees | Justin Welsh (Solopreneur)
sources.summary: Justin Welsh explains his move from burned-out VP of Sales to a zero-employee business. He covers auditing your time with Pareto, finding a niche, validating by serving 5-10 people one-on-one, using an enemy to build a movement, and a four-step funnel. He also argues for staying specific as an audience grows.

principles.text: Audit your week: rank tasks by impact per hour, focus on the top 20%, and simplify, automate, delegate or eliminate the rest.
principles.quote: you should probably be spending your time doing the 20% of things that maximize 80% of your intended outcome

principles.text: Validate a business by serving 5-10 people one-on-one; if they spend money and time and get results, productize it.
principles.quote: identify five to 10 people who have those problems have those aspirations and want to work with you right and are they willing to put some skin in the game

principles.text: Pick an enemy (an ideology or status quo) to build a movement; marketing works by helping people throw rocks at a common enemy.
principles.quote: once you have an enemy you can build a movement because movements are built by defeating another enemy

principles.text: Keep the funnel simple: get discovered via organic social, build trust with long-form content, deepen relationships for pricey offers, then monetize.
principles.quote: it's get discovered build trust deepen relationships and monetize very simple

principles.text: Stay specific as your audience grows; a niche audience lets you ladder from micro offer to core product to high ticket sooner.
principles.quote: as you grow a specific audience your options are more plentiful right so you can do things like create a micro offer

principles.text: Use AI to analyze your posts, articles and sales data for patterns, and keep the creative work yourself.
principles.quote: keep your creativity let it manage the data

sources.title: Justin Welsh: Building a non-scalable 7-figure solo business, funnel, pricing and channel stacking
sources.originalTitle: Justin Welsh: Why I Built a Non-Scalable 7-Figure Business
sources.summary: Justin explains why he intentionally keeps his business non-scalable, prioritizing profit and lifestyle over revenue and headcount. He walks through his simple content-to-newsletter-to-product funnel, incremental low-price product ladder, purchasing power parity, and a bolt-on channel strategy that adds platforms one at a time.

principles.text: Optimize for profit, margins and lifestyle rather than revenue; a solo, intentionally non-scalable business can be plenty.
principles.quote: I think less about revenue. I think more about profit. I think about margins. And I think about really lifestyle first, business second.

principles.text: Run a dead-simple funnel: social for discovery, newsletter for expertise and authority, then a product offer.
principles.quote: Social media is discovery. It's awareness of my brand.

principles.text: Start with a cheap first product as a trust tripwire, then sell higher-priced offers to that goodwill-rich customer pool.
principles.quote: I called it my trust trip wire.

principles.text: Use a main product as a Trojan horse to a low-cost monthly continuity offer for ongoing downstream revenue.
principles.quote: I want to use my main product as a Trojan horse to something else

principles.text: Build small, outcomes-based courses that solve one narrow problem and unlock a wider, pricier one.
principles.quote: think incrementally. What's that early narrow problem that people need to solve in order to unlock a wider and more expensive problem down the road?

principles.text: Maximize one channel first, then open a secondary channel and rerun the same playbook; stacking channels makes a business predictable.
principles.quote: I maximized my primary channel first and then I opened up a secondary channel.

sources.title: Justin Welsh on burnout, five-year work cycles and building a solo business around your life
sources.originalTitle: Taking Ownership of Your Life — Justin Welsh
sources.summary: In conversation with Paul Millerd, Justin Welsh explains how he burned out as a sales exec, then built a solo business with control over his own outcomes. He covers LinkedIn timing, working with a specialist partner on launches, and keeping the business from becoming a job.

principles.text: Burnout comes from losing control of outcomes, not from working hard.
principles.quote: I don't think of burnout as working too hard I mean I can work hard I can work hard right now and not burn out if I'm loving what I'm doing

principles.text: A solo business removes deadline-driven problem stacking; you choose urgency and own outcomes.
principles.quote: problems didn't compound because problems didn't have a deadline

principles.text: Starting a platform early compounds: four years of LinkedIn posting built the audience before pivoting to solopreneurship.
principles.quote: by the time I started talking about solopreneurship which wasn't until like 2022 I had already been writing on LinkedIn for 4 years

principles.text: Delegate systems work to a specialist you trust, but never outsource the creative work.
principles.quote: you can Outsource a few things but the one thing I never want to Outsource is creative and so I love writing I love doing the videos I love building my products

principles.text: Teach decision-making, not paint-by-numbers steps, because businesses don't get built from one script.
principles.quote: it's not like do this step one do this step two paint by numbers because businesses don't get built that way

principles.text: Guard against building yourself a job: cap the work week at three days and keep engagement light.
principles.quote: I've reduced myself down to a 3-day work week this year

sources.title: How Justin Welsh built a LinkedIn, Twitter and email audience: the creator funnel and one-platform-first approach
sources.originalTitle: The SECRET to building your business on LinkedIn and Twitter | Justin Welsh
sources.summary: Justin explains how he grew on LinkedIn by writing daily, then used that audience to bootstrap Twitter and a newsletter. He lays out his creator funnel (awareness, trust, deepening relationship, monetization), why a narrow niche and real craft matter, and how he pre-sells cheap, fast products based on audience demand.

principles.text: Pick one platform you enjoy and master it before adding others; skills transfer and make the next platform faster.
principles.quote: pick one platform that you like to be on so the biggest thing i see is like i heard tik tok is popular should i be on it well do you like doing videos no then no like do what you like to do

principles.text: Run a creator funnel: awareness, then trust (newsletter), then deepening relationships (community), then monetization.
principles.quote: i think of that awareness and discovery at the top trust building in the middle and then relationship deepening in the end and i think if you do those things really effectively you're able to build a really great business

principles.text: Stay in the awareness and trust phase longer before selling; a large audience of the right people gives enormous leverage.
principles.quote: stick to growing that awareness and that trust before you monetize or build a community or anything like that

principles.text: Get narrow: say one thing a thousand ways so readers instantly self-select in or out of your content.
principles.quote: learn how to say one thing a thousand ways it's better than saying a thousand things one way

principles.text: Use your existing audience to seed a new platform, then siphon followers into an email list you own.
principles.quote: i would pull 50 000 people out of their inbox and into a tweet thread and that was able for me to sort of get that tweet thread moving

principles.text: Pre-sell products and only build once enough people have paid; build what customers ask for, not what you want.
principles.quote: i never build anything unless i make a certain amount of money on it and i'll go out and say this is coming in 45 days like it's on sale right now grab it and as soon as i cross a threshold i'll go out and build it

sources.title: Justin Welsh: Optimize for time, not scale, and play the long game
sources.originalTitle: Justin Welsh: You Don't Need Scale To Be Happy | The Danny Miranda Podcast 298
sources.summary: Justin Welsh explains why he built a one-person business around time, family and experiences rather than scale. He covers anti-goals, shutting down a working community, course design and pricing, borrowing proven formats to grow on Twitter, and acting today instead of perfecting.

principles.text: Treat building a brand as a decades-long journey, so short-term dips in engagement don't derail pivots.
principles.quote: I think of this as like a decades-long journey not like what happens on Thursday compared to Wednesday is is irrelevant to me

principles.text: Stack transferable skills (action, clear communication, ego control) so you can go in any direction with confidence.
principles.quote: getting one percent better at 17 different things all the time and uh you blink and suddenly you're a much more well-rounded marketer content creator business person

principles.text: Use anti-goals: decide what you don't want to do, then cut it. Narrowing niche and raising rates opens time that finds new revenue.
principles.quote: an idea of like an anti-goal isn't like this is the goal I want to achieve it's like this is the stuff I don't want to do next year

principles.text: Shut down even a profitable product if it conflicts with your values, and don't automatically refill the freed time.
principles.quote: my goal wasn't to like see a free Gap and fill it yeah that would have defeated the purpose of what I was doing

principles.text: Define riches as time, friends, family and experiences; once income is enough, you don't need to 2x or 5x it.
principles.quote: I don't need to scale I don't need to 2x I don't need to 5x like if it just stays consistent for the next 10 to 20 years I'll be thrilled

principles.text: Price a course as an impulse buy that still feels worth using, and treat it as a Trojan horse for a later premium product.
principles.quote: it's affordable enough to make it an Impulse buy but it's expensive enough where like you don't really want to waste 150 bucks

sources.title: Justin Welsh: Build a business from a bleeding-neck problem, marketing, and an offer
sources.originalTitle: The Simplest Way to Build a Business That Lasts with Justin Welsh
sources.summary: Justin Welsh explains how he left his job with runway, a pre-built pipeline and intact relationships, and what a business needs: a deeply understood painful problem, a way to get attention, and a differentiated offer. He also shares how he tracks his business (visitors to intended page) and a customer-research action step.

principles.text: A business needs three things: a painful problem, a way to get attention, and a differentiated offer. Two of three is a hobby.
principles.quote: If you have those three things, deeply understanding your bleeding neck problem of your audience, having a a a unique and differentiating way to solve that problem, and then being able to talk about that and get attention for it. If you can do those three things, you have a business.

principles.text: Target a 'bleeding neck' problem: one so painful people pay today. Dig past surface problems to the dollar and emotional cost.
principles.quote: you have to find a problem in your target audience that people are willing to pay for today because it is so painful to solve

principles.text: Painful problems usually involve saving time, making or saving money, being accepted, or improving relationships.
principles.quote: generally it relates to saving time, making money or saving money, being accepted, right? Or improving relationships.

principles.text: If it doesn't keep customers up at night, it isn't a bleeding neck problem. Frame the problem in their concrete stakes.
principles.quote: Nobody goes to bed and can't sleep having nightmares about better team communication.

principles.text: Track visitors to the intended place (the offer or signup page) as the key KPI, since it predicts sales.
principles.quote: the best key performance indicator for my business is simply visitors to intended place.

principles.text: Before going solo: save runway, build pipeline first, leave without burning bridges, and have a risk plan.
principles.quote: I built my runway and I built my business, you know, going out on a limb with a risk reduction plan. So like if this fails then this, if this fails, then this.

sources.title: How Justin Welsh grows and monetizes a LinkedIn audience: sub-niche, content, tribe, leads
sources.originalTitle: Live Workshop - Justin Welsh - How to Grow & Monetize Your LinkedIn Audience
sources.summary: Justin walks through his four-part LinkedIn playbook: pick a tight sub-niche, create content that moves people into your tribe (not dopamine-driven engagement), build a relevant audience by leading, curating or interviewing, then turn it into leads via an inbound email funnel and outbound congratulation outreach. He stresses patience over get-rich-quick schemes.

principles.text: Pick one sub-niche and talk about it every day so people know what you teach.
principles.quote: people should know exactly who you serve and exactly how you help them

principles.text: Narrow broad topic to niche to sub-niche; aim for 100 to 1,000 true fans, not something too specific.
principles.quote: if you can get 100 to 1000 true fans you can build a business

principles.text: Optimize for customers and dollars, not likes. Feel-good viral content irrelevant to your business doesn't sell.
principles.quote: it's dollars over dopamine

principles.text: Move people into your tribe by polarizing, teaching and entertaining; accept that some will dislike your content.
principles.quote: content that 100 of people like is generally not that interesting content that zero percent of people like is probably pretty mean

principles.text: You don't need to be a world expert; create for the you of two to three years ago and stay just ahead of your students.
principles.quote: create content for the you from two to three years ago

principles.text: Pull people off the platform into an email list using a top-of-funnel evergreen guide and a bottom-of-funnel offer, then send a consistent newsletter.
principles.quote: i actually want to pull people off of linkedin because the linkedin algorithm can change any minute any hour any day

sources.title: How Justin Welsh runs a one-person content business on a 10-step system
sources.originalTitle: Justin Welsh: The Operating System He Used To Conquer LinkedIn
sources.summary: Justin explains how he built a Notion-based content operating system that turns one newsletter into 28 weekly pieces, why he shut down a profitable paid community, and how LinkedIn and Twitter differ. Core lessons: systematize away friction, price for optionality, and optimize for money rather than impressions.

principles.text: Build systems iteratively: every time you hit friction, add a step to the system.
principles.quote: any time that i come up against friction my brain says like how do you systematize removing friction

principles.text: Use a hub-and-spoke model: one long-form newsletter is the hub, and everything else is derived from it.
principles.quote: how can i systematize turning that newsletter into 10 to 20 unique ideas

principles.text: Push one idea through many lenses (story, contrarian take, listicle, teardown) to say the same thing a thousand ways.
principles.quote: learn how to say the same thing a thousand different ways and when you can say the same thing a thousand different ways you can create a bunch of different content

principles.text: Systems should be format-based, not topic-based, so any topic can drop into them.
principles.quote: every process has a template

principles.text: Optimize for money, not impressions: put links in posts even though reach drops, because click-through multiplies.
principles.quote: my business doesn't run on impressions my business runs on money

principles.text: Price memberships quarterly: it commits members long enough to get value while limiting the creator's lock-in.
principles.quote: quarterly memberships are the sweet spot

sources.title: Content Systems: how Justin Welsh runs a one-person content engine from newsletter hub to social spokes
sources.summary: Justin explains how he built a solo content system: start with a 30-minute daily habit, add structure each time friction appears, and write one newsletter that gets chopped into many social posts. He also covers niching down and low-friction pricing that follows discovery then trust.

principles.text: Start your content system as a daily 30-minute block, then add tools each time friction appears.
principles.quote: system creation is an iterative process it starts very simply and every time that you hit that block and new friction appears you introduce something new to remove that friction

principles.text: Make a newsletter the pillar piece, then chop it into 5-7 social posts that link back to it.
principles.quote: I ideate I think of an idea and I write a newsletter about it once I've written the newsletter I chop my newsletter into five to seven pieces of content

principles.text: Ideate on a schedule and keep a growing bank of ideas so you never face a blank page.
principles.quote: my goal is to create anywhere from six to ten UniQue Ideas each week when I only need one so I constantly have a growing Repository

principles.text: Use a repeatable copywriting template for every newsletter so writing stays easy.
principles.quote: my newsletter every single week gets pushed through the same template I introduce a problem I introduce why it's important I introduce how most people try and solve the problem

principles.text: Niche down so you're the only one, and offer a non-obvious solution to an obvious problem.
principles.quote: start by saying how can I Niche down so that I'm close to the only or one of five or one of ten people and then how do I bring in non-obvious solution to the table

principles.text: Move people from discovery to trust, then price products as low-friction impulse buys.
principles.quote: I move them from Discovery to trust and then at the end I use pricing that makes it an Impulse Buy

sources.title: How Justin Welsh built a $10M solo business in 23 steps
sources.summary: Justin Welsh walks through the 23 steps from posting daily on LinkedIn to $10M in total revenue, with no paid ads and no employees. The path runs from noise to signal, a high-touch service business, a cheap trust-building product, then audience, community, newsletter, sponsorships and a flagship launch.

principles.text: Create lots of content early; volume finds your voice and shows what resonates.
principles.quote: The key here isn't perfection. It's volume. You need to create enough content to find your voice and see what resonates.

principles.text: Start with a high-touch service business to learn the market and get immediate cash flow.
principles.quote: Your first business should be a high-touch, high-value service, because you’ll learn so much about your market from talking to customers. Plus, you generate immediate cash flow.

principles.text: Niche down once you know which customers you serve best.
principles.quote: The riches are in the niches, and you can't niche down until you know who you serve best.

principles.text: Raise rates as results improve, and optimize for time, not just money.
principles.quote: Higher rates = better clients = better results = even higher rates.

principles.text: Let customers tell you what to build next, and test first products quickly and cheaply.
principles.quote: Your customers will tell you what to build next. You just have to listen.

principles.text: Price low to build trust, then raise prices as you deliver results.
principles.quote: Price low to build trust, then raise prices as you deliver results.

sources.title: What $3.4M in course sales taught Justin Welsh: build in public, price low, show testimonials
sources.summary: Justin shares five lessons from his digital course business: building in public, accessible pricing that fuels word-of-mouth, testimonials as the best promotion, an 80/20 give/ask content ratio, and short courses that people finish. Each lesson is backed by his own revenue, conversion and completion numbers.

principles.text: Build your product in public so your audience is invested before launch.
principles.quote: Both products generated roughly the same amount of landing page views, but The LinkedIn Operating System converted 2.7x higher even with 3x the cost, partly because people could see what I was building, and were invested in the journey.

principles.text: Price products accessibly to create a word-of-mouth and affiliate engine.
principles.quote: This is why I recommend that people price things to be accessible and create a WOM machine. It's easy to recommend a $150 product to your friends.

principles.text: High-ticket offers demand heavy trust and nurturing that a small audience can't supply.
principles.quote: The amount of trust and nurturing needed to get someone into a high-ticket deal like that is pretty massive, IMO.

principles.text: Share customer testimonials regularly; customers' words convert better than your own.
principles.quote: The words of your customers will always convert prospects at a much higher rate than your own. Every beautiful testimonial is a chance to convert more prospects into happy customers.

principles.text: Give value at least 80% of the time and promote 20% or less.
principles.quote: The golden rule that I've found to be effective is to make sure that you are giving value 80% of the time or more and promoting 20% of the time or less.

principles.text: Keep courses short when starting out to boost completion and adoption.
principles.quote: Teach people what they want to learn in 45 minutes or less, and you'll increase your completion and adoption rate.

sources.title: How Justin Welsh writes LinkedIn posts: meat, trailer, then TL;DR + CTC
sources.summary: Justin Welsh shares a three-step writing process behind his LinkedIn growth. He writes the informational "meat" first, then a "trailer" that breaks the scroll and hooks readers before "see more", then closes with a TL;DR and call-to-conversation to drive comments. A typical post of his earns around 230k views and hundreds of comments.

principles.text: Write the substance first: decide what you're teaching, showing or suggesting before polishing the hook.
principles.quote: The first thing I do is create "the meat" of the content. This is where you’re teaching, showing, or suggesting something.

principles.text: A great post is useless if nobody stops to read it, so you have to break the scroll pattern.
principles.quote: People might find these suggestions helpful. But they’ll never see them if they don’t stop to read the content.

principles.text: The trailer has two jobs: break the scroll with line one, and make every line intriguing enough to pull the reader to the next.
principles.quote: Break the scroll pattern with the first line.

principles.text: Know your audience to write a good first line: use short, consumable lines and a big number they care about.
principles.quote: Part of writing a good first line is knowing your audience. **What do they care about?**

principles.text: The last line before "see more" is where readers commit or keep scrolling, so it must create intrigue by promising something to learn.
principles.quote: It absolutely must be intriguing. I create intrigue by promising that they are going to learn a few things related to the $1.5M in course sales.

principles.text: End with a TL;DR summary plus a call-to-conversation so readers can join the comments without rereading the post.
principles.quote: After the TL;DR, I use a CTC (call-to-conversation) which increases the likelihood that the reader will leave a comment and give the post more traction.

sources.title: How to write a viral LinkedIn post: the 3-line opener template (enemy, hero, gasoline)
sources.summary: Justin breaks down the opener of his most successful LinkedIn post (4.766M impressions) into a reusable three-line template. Only 210 characters show above "see more", so the opener works like a thread hook: stop the scroll, flip the script, then add gasoline and a teaser. He turns every post that performs well into a template and reuses it.

principles.text: Treat the 210 characters above "see more" as the whole job: get people interested enough to click.
principles.quote: You have 210 characters to get people interested in the rest of it.

principles.text: The first line matters more than almost everything else in the post, so make it excellent.
principles.quote: The first line is more important than 95% of the rest of the post.

principles.text: Open by attacking a relatable enemy your audience already dislikes, using a negative word.
principles.quote: So for the first line of this post, I chose what I call a "relatable enemy" and then "threw rocks" at it.

principles.text: Flip the script: after the enemy line, name the hero (the opposite) and say it is gaining ground.
principles.quote: I choose the hero (the opposite of the enemy) and tell them that the hero is gaining ground.

principles.text: End the opener with a gasoline line plus a simple teaser question that earns the "see more" click.
principles.quote: The last line in your opener must take the frenzied reader and hook them into clicking "see more".

principles.text: Turn every post that performs well into a template and reuse it many times.
principles.quote: For every post that I create that performs well, I analyze the post, turn it into a template, and reuse it multiple times.

sources.title: How Justin Welsh reverse engineers LinkedIn posts with data instead of guessing
sources.summary: Justin breaks every LinkedIn post into four parts (opener, body, call-to-conversation, image) and tracks a specific metric for each in Taplio. He studies his top 10 posts per metric to find patterns, then re-tests quarterly. He reports a 28.7% quarter-over-quarter engagement lift and follower growth from 586,000 to over 645,000 in 90 days.

principles.text: Guessing is not a strategy; track post data and let it guide what you publish.
principles.quote: They're playing a guessing game. And guessing is not a strategy.

principles.text: Break each post into four components and track a specific metric for each one.
principles.quote: I break down every LinkedIn post I create into four key components:

principles.text: Judge openers by impressions: study what your top 10 posts by impressions have in common.
principles.quote: I like to start by looking at my top 10 LinkedIn posts by impressions and the type of openers I used to get a sense for what’s working.

principles.text: Use likes as a proxy for readers finishing the body, then study length and structure of top posts.
principles.quote: If more people like a post, then they likely read it to the end. That means I did something right.

principles.text: Specific questions tied to personal experience drive more and better comments than generic asks.
principles.quote: I find that posts with specific questions that tap into people's personal experiences get more comments than others. And the comments tend to be more thoughtful.

principles.text: What works for you may differ and the algorithm changes: run your own tests and adjust quarterly.
principles.quote: The LinkedIn algorithm evolves. Keep testing, and adjust quarterly.

sources.title: The 5 Phases of Solopreneurship: what to focus on at each stage
sources.summary: Justin Welsh breaks solo business growth into five phases: stay alive, build systems, growth focused, invest in defense, automate. Each phase calls for different work, and spending limited time on the wrong tasks for your phase is the main risk. Each phase typically takes a year or two, so patience is the differentiator.

principles.text: Match your work to your phase; doing the wrong tasks for your stage burns limited solo time and energy.
principles.quote: it’s especially important for a solopreneur to spend your limited time and energy on the appropriate tasks for your phase.

principles.text: In phase 1, survive: keep expenses low and use free social platforms instead of ads.
principles.quote: Social media is basically free. Use platforms like Twitter and (especially) LinkedIn to share your knowledge and expertise. The only investment here is your time. Stay away from ads and expensive marketing campaigns.

principles.text: Once you have traction, document repeatable tasks as systems so they can be followed or delegated.
principles.quote: Every task you find yourself doing repeatedly can potentially be systematized.

principles.text: Invest in growth only after systems exist: expand to new channels and partnerships.
principles.quote: Once you have systems in place, it’s much easier to put some “additional weight” on the foundation of your business.

principles.text: Successful solo businesses attract copycats, so build a moat: stronger brand, SEO, email automation, less reliance on social.
principles.quote: Instead of relying so heavily on social media, I’ll be playing defense by actively investing in things that give me more of a “moat”.

principles.text: Use paid ads only once systems, brand and landing pages convert; target spending $1 to make $2.
principles.quote: Ultimately, you want to get to a place where you’re spending $1 to generate $2.

sources.title: The 1-3-5 Method: How 1 pillar piece of content becomes 16
sources.summary: Welsh explains his 1-3-5 content method: create one deep pillar piece, extract three core ideas, and turn each into five micro-pieces. It lets creators produce consistent, varied content across formats without burning out, since results matter more than hours spent.

principles.text: Creators are rewarded for results, not hours, so be efficient with content effort.
principles.quote: Because we aren’t rewarded by the hours we spend, we’re rewarded by the results we produce. So we have to be smart and efficient with our efforts.

principles.text: Start with one deep pillar piece on a big audience pain point; it makes all other content faster.
principles.quote: Creating this pillar piece of content will be the hardest part of the process. But it makes rest of the content production much faster and easier.

principles.text: Extract three standalone core ideas from the pillar piece.
principles.quote: Next, you want to extract three main concepts or tips from your pillar piece. These should be substantial enough to stand alone as valuable content.

principles.text: Turn each core idea into five micro pieces across formats: written posts, short video, carousel, poll.
principles.quote: Now, for **each** of your three core ideas, you’ll create five pieces of micro-content:

principles.text: Repurposing one deep piece across formats keeps your message consistent while adding variety.
principles.quote: You’re beating the same drum with some variety. This will naturally reinforce your brand and your message.

principles.text: Multiple formats meet audience members where they prefer to consume content.
principles.quote: The 1-3-5 method meets people where they consume best.

sources.title: Passive selling: turn social attention into asset sales via a hook-body-CTA-article micro-funnel
sources.summary: Justin lays out a data-driven system for keeping digital product sales going after launch without hard-selling on social. Track hooks, body copy and CTAs to find winning combos, send traffic to relevant articles instead of the homepage, and end each article with a soft CTA to the product.

principles.text: Post-launch sales longevity, not the launch, is what makes a digital asset valuable.
principles.quote: while having a successful course or book launch is important, maintaining sales (post-launch) is what makes an asset so valuable.

principles.text: Skip the hard sell on social; get enough relevant people in front of your product without saying 'buy this'.
principles.quote: there’s a better way to ‘sell’ without actually asking people to buy in your social content.

principles.text: Move people from short-form social to your website, where you can educate them on the problem.
principles.quote: my process is to get people to my website, where I can further educate them on the problem they’re trying to solve.

principles.text: Break social content into hook, body and CTA, and track each: the hook drives most impressions.
principles.quote: The hook on your social content is generally what leads to 90% of your success in terms of impressions

principles.text: After 3-6 months of publishing, identify your top five hooks, bodies and CTAs and combine the winners.
principles.quote: After three to six months of publishing content, you should have a good sense of your top five hooks, body styles, and calls-to-action.

principles.text: Send traffic to relevant articles, not the homepage, and end each with a passive CTA to your asset; rotate ~20 articles and track reader-to-buyer conversion.
principles.quote: These articles are like 24/7/365 salespeople that cost you nothing other than the time it takes to write them.

sources.title: How to build a lead magnet that gives everything away: solve the 'early narrow' problem
sources.summary: Justin Welsh argues that lead magnets which teach 10% and sell 90% feel like a trick and erode trust. Instead, map your customer's journey, pick an early, narrow step that unlocks the rest, solve it completely for free, and then sell the remainder of the journey.

principles.text: Withholding real information in a lead magnet feels like a trick and destroys the trust you've built.
principles.quote: People can tell when you’re holding back the real information and that can feel like a trick. And once people feel tricked? That erodes any trust you’ve built with them.

principles.text: Start by listing every step your customer must get right to reach their big goal, in logical order.
principles.quote: Make a list of everything your ideal customer needs to figure out in order to accomplish their big goal. And then organize your list by the most logical steps.

principles.text: Pick an 'early narrow' problem: a crucial early step that, once solved, unlocks the rest of the journey.
principles.quote: This is a problem that, when solved, unlocks the rest of the ‘wider journey’ for your customer.

principles.text: Solve the narrow problem 100% and give it away generously; you keep your promise and no one is tricked.
principles.quote: Design a lead magnet that 100% solves that narrow problem. And give it all away generously.

principles.text: Solving the first step makes you a trusted guide and the logical choice for the rest of the journey.
principles.quote: You’re now the logical choice to continue working with to get even better. You’ve demonstrated your expertise, helped your potential customer, and built trust early on.

principles.text: Sell the remaining journey at the end of the lead magnet, via a simple video, email series, or inside the magnet itself.
principles.quote: Sell the remainder of the journey in a simple video, email series, or inside of your lead magnet.

sources.title: Digital leverage: Think 1x, publish 10x, sell 100x, compound 1,000x
sources.summary: Justin Welsh explains "digital leverage" as using the internet to get more output with less time and effort. The system has three stages: turn one idea into one long-form piece and about 10 social posts, use those posts to passively sell, then compound sales with a generous affiliate program.

principles.text: Win with leverage, not brute force; hustle-24/7 culture is a trap for a team of one.
principles.quote: The biggest flaw of the 24/7 hustle culture is the misconception that if you work hard enough, you will succeed in the end.You win with leverage.Not brute force.

principles.text: Start from one strong idea, make one robust long-form piece, then break it into smaller posts for each platform.
principles.quote: After I choose a topic to write about, I create one robust, long-form piece of content

principles.text: Find ideas by spending an hour a day on trends, industry insights and social engagement.
principles.quote: I research trending topics, read industry insights, and engage on social media for an hour every day.

principles.text: More free, valuable touch points build trust and authority, so audiences buy your paid offers.
principles.quote: Because the more your audience values your free content, the more likely they are to invest in your paid offerings.

principles.text: Sell passively: use bite-sized posts as a trojan horse linking to your site, testimonials or articles that lead to your products.
principles.quote: This is what I call "passive selling" and it works much better, IMO, than aggressively promoting yourself all the time.

principles.text: Compound sales with a generous affiliate program; Justin pays 35% instead of the standard 20% so people feel empowered to earn.
principles.quote: I made the decision to pay 35% rather than the standard 20% simply because I want people to feel empowered to earn.

sources.title: How to build your first online business from scratch: Justin Welsh's 7-step playbook
sources.summary: Justin Welsh lays out 7 steps he'd follow to start an online business from zero: pick one problem for one specific group, package a clear roadmap, ship a simple $50-$150 product fast, find customers on a few channels, collect testimonials, and build a repeatable selling system backed by simple daily-sales math.

principles.text: Start with one problem for one specific group, ideally one you solved yourself years ago.
principles.quote: You need one problem that one very specific group of people have in common.

principles.text: Sell a roadmap from point A to point B, not a broad education; people want one problem solved.
principles.quote: We overestimate how much people want to learn at once.

principles.text: Product format matters less than finishing it; timebox the build with a hard deadline.
principles.quote: It doesn't matter what format, it just matters that you'll complete it.

principles.text: Use simple hosting and a $50-$150 price at first; get complicated later, make sales now.
principles.quote: Charge between $50 and $150 for your product. That's affordable enough to get buyers without building trust for many years.

principles.text: Test several distribution channels, find the one that leads to sales, then triple down on it.
principles.quote: You want to find which of these channels leads to sales and then triple down.

principles.text: Back into revenue goals with daily sales and traffic targets, and separate content that earns attention from content that converts.
principles.quote: Find 4 people who will buy your $75 course each day.

sources.title: How to find your first 1,000 true fans: niche, category pirate, story, unscalable work
sources.summary: Justin Welsh lays out a four-step growth plan for building an audience from zero: pick a tight niche, hold a non-obvious point of view, tell a real backstory, and do unscalable work early. He backs it with his own routine of daily posting, replying to every comment and DM, and hundreds of Zoom calls with followers.

principles.text: Serve a very specific person with very specific advice; niche content cuts through generic noise.
principles.quote: You can't just "help small businesses". You're much better off helping "SaaS companies in the finance vertical, below $10M in revenue".

principles.text: Stand out with non-obvious content and a unique viewpoint; repeating what others say makes you a commodity.
principles.quote: Remember, that if you just say what other people are saying, you become a commodity.

principles.text: Stress-test your unique perspective with sharp questions about what everyone believes, what nobody discusses, and what mistakes people miss.
principles.quote: What is something everyone believes to be true, that you don't?

principles.text: A real, compelling backstory acts like gasoline on your growth; audiences must see themselves in you.
principles.quote: They need to literally see themselves in you.

principles.text: Your story must be true, but structured so it is easy and exciting to follow.
principles.quote: The story can't be made up or fake. It should be your real story but stitched together in a fashion that makes it easy (and exciting) to follow along.

principles.text: Early on, do things that don't scale: post daily, answer every comment and DM, comment on others' content, meet followers.
principles.quote: I cannot overstate how important it is to be everywhere when you're just getting started.

sources.title: Justin Welsh's Friday weekly preview: 8 questions to audit your calendar
sources.summary: Justin shares his Friday ritual for planning the week ahead using eight questions. The process eliminates, automates and delegates low-value work, protects time for creative work, family and fun, and keeps a one-person business aligned with his values and goals.

principles.text: Eliminate first: remove calendar items that don't serve your bigger goals.
principles.quote: Elimination is your best friend as a Solopreneur or Creator. Look ahead to make sure you’re not wasting time doing things that don’t support your goals.

principles.text: Automate repetitive workflows end to end, like sponsorship sales, to reclaim time and mental energy.
principles.quote: Buy button → Submission of Copy → Calendar Invite → Newsletter Publication

principles.text: Delegate tasks that cost more time than they're worth, and do it sooner than feels necessary.
principles.quote: Delegation is about recognizing the value of your time and passing off tasks that cost you more time than they’re worth.

principles.text: Don't mistake urgent for important; push non-critical meetings 60-90 days out.
principles.quote: If a meeting isn’t important at this very moment, I push it 60-90 days down the road to make space for things that are urgent AND important.

principles.text: Shorten meetings by demanding an agenda and capping durations; most can be halved.
principles.quote: Most meetings can be halved in length without losing substance or outcomes.

principles.text: Run a regular weekly review so the calendar reflects your values and goals, including deliberate fun and family time.
principles.quote: It’s making sure my calendar is aligned with my values, goals, and the realities of running a one-person business.

sources.title: From 7 years of failure to a $4M business: a 4-step LinkedIn plan to find a niche and build an audience
sources.summary: Justin lays out what he'd do if starting over today: pick a niche at the intersection of skill, passion and willingness to pay, post with a "Teach, Teach, Teach, Sell" mix, comment on 9 relevant posts daily, and use analytics to adjust. Built for LinkedIn but works on other platforms.

principles.text: Pick a niche where what you're good at, what you love, and what people will pay for overlap.
principles.quote: Start by identifying the intersection of something you’re good at, something you love to do, and something people are willing to pay you for.

principles.text: Add a distinctive angle to your niche, like serving a specific type of person, to stand out.
principles.quote: Your niche could be ‘Confident Public Speaking for Introverted Professionals.’

principles.text: Use a Teach, Teach, Teach, Sell content mix: 80% value, 20% soft promotion.
principles.quote: 80% of the time you’ll provide value to your audience. And 20% of the time, you’ll softly promote your expertise, products, or services.

principles.text: Consistent teaching content builds the trust, expertise and authority needed to generate leads.
principles.quote: If you follow this 5-post cycle consistently, you'll establish the trust, expertise, and authority I talk about so often.

principles.text: Comment thoughtfully on 9 relevant posts daily to build visibility and relationships, for a year.
principles.quote: My 18 cent strategy just means leaving your two cents on 9 relevant posts per day.

principles.text: Track what works, adjust content to data and feedback, and ask people when you don't know what they want.
principles.quote: And if you don’t know what people want, ask them.

sources.title: Reverse engineering attention in 2025: pattern break, relevance snap, emotional accuracy
sources.summary: Justin argues attention is three things working together, not just a great hook. After 4,000+ pieces of content, he found you need a pattern disruption, a relevance snap (this is about me), and emotional accuracy (specific, real moments over stats). Miss one and you are noise in the feed.

principles.text: Attention isn't one thing: it takes pattern disruption, relevance snap and emotional accuracy together.
principles.quote: attention isn't one thing.** It's three different things working together. And if you miss any of them, you're just more noise in someone's feed.

principles.text: Open by breaking the reader's mental pattern with something that makes their brain stutter.
principles.quote: First, you need pattern disruption…something that makes a person's brain stutter.

principles.text: The relevance snap shifts content from a general topic to the reader's own specific experience.
principles.quote: It's when your content shifts from being about a general topic to being about the reader's specific experience.

principles.text: Write to make people feel seen, not to sound smart; specific, vulnerable moments beat stats.
principles.quote: They write to sound smart when they should write to make people feel seen.

principles.text: It isn't clickbait if you deliver, so you can start with polarizing pattern disruption.
principles.quote: Something isn't clickbait if you deliver.

principles.text: You compete with the scroll-skim-forget reflex, so engineer the complete experience, not one tactic.
principles.quote: You're not really competing with other specific creators anymore. You're competing with the scroll-skim-forget reflex that everyone's developed.

sources.title: Delete some of your offers: why fewer products and one price per offer sell more
sources.summary: Justin argues that too many offers and price tiers cause decision fatigue and quietly kill sales. He recommends one course, one community and one service, each with a single price, so customers only choose how they want to "do it": alone, with others, or done for them.

principles.text: Too many options cause decision fatigue, and people then choose nothing.
principles.quote: Decision fatigue happens when too many options wear out your brain, making it difficult to actually make a choice.

principles.text: Give each course a single price instead of tiers or bundles.
principles.quote: And this is exactly why each of the courses I offer has one price. That's it.

principles.text: Sell one service tailored to common client needs: take it or leave it.
principles.quote: When I offered consulting back in the day, I had one offer tailored to the most common needs of my clients. Take it or leave it.

principles.text: Keep it to one course, one community and one service; at most add an accelerated service or a mastermind tier.
principles.quote: But, honestly? Most of the time, one course, one community, and one service is perfect.

principles.text: One of each product forms a natural value ladder; customers only choose how they want to do it.
principles.quote: This means that your customers only have to choose how they want to "do it."

principles.text: Every added option adds a decision point that slows buyers and invites more questions.
principles.quote: Every option you add to your offering creates another decision point for your customer.

sources.title: How Justin Welsh got 870 subscribers by moving the CTA link into a second Tweet
sources.summary: When Twitter's algorithm change capped his daily newsletter signups at about 250, Welsh ran an experiment: the 1-Tweet CTA vs. the 2-Tweet CTA. He moved the link into a second Tweet so the first could reach people without a link. The lesson is to keep testing as algorithms shift.

principles.text: Keep experimenting on social media and in your business; testing and measuring is how you learn what works.
principles.quote: I’m always testing and measuring and modifying my strategies.

principles.text: Don't wait for a platform to go back to normal after an algorithm change; run an experiment to recover results.
principles.quote: I knew a lot of things were changing at Twitter, but I wasn’t willing to wait around and hope things would go back to “normal.”

principles.text: Platforms tend to suppress posts with links, so move the CTA link out of the main post and into a follow-up reply.
principles.quote: I simply moved my CTA (the link) to the 2nd Tweet, resulting in a tiny thread of two short Tweets.

principles.text: Splitting reach from the CTA worked: the link-free first Tweet drove reach, the second drove signups.
principles.quote: The first part had no CTA, and it generated 802K impressions.

principles.text: Social algorithms are always moving, so creators must keep adapting and experimenting.
principles.quote: Just remember, social media algorithms are always on the move.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Justin Welsh explains how he went from burned-out SaaS executive to a one-person business by writing daily on LinkedIn and turning that attention into low-priced products and a community. He covers his post structure, pricing, and why he starts with a service business before productizing.

chunks.heading: Starting a one-person business: service first, then product
chunks.text:
Justin's core sequence for a beginner:

1. Pick the people you like spending time with. "Misery doesn't scale."
2. Choose people 2-3 years behind you in their journey (e.g. a sales manager helping account executives who want to become managers).
3. Talk to them for free for 15 minutes and learn what blocks them.
4. Sell a service first. He prefers a simple coaching business, with a no-brainer price such as 100 dollars for an hour.
5. Sell to about 20 people. That is 2,000 dollars, and it shows the most common, most painful problem.
6. Find the one fix that works every time, then turn it into a self-guided product (e.g. "become a sales manager in 90 days").
7. Raise service rates once the product exists, from 100 to about 250 an hour.
8. Send people who can't afford the service to the product, and people who don't want to self-learn to the service.
9. Repeat with other groups. The end state is about five impulse-buy products and five higher-ticket service offers.

He says he is "a big fan of service before product" because the service teaches you what the product should be. He turned his own service businesses into products this way.

chunks.heading: Why a one-person business is mostly marketing
chunks.text:
- The most common misconception: having a niche and a solution is "only two pieces of the pie."
- The missing piece is attention: people knowing who you are, what you do and why.
- That means copywriting, hosting podcasts or live video, running YouTube, building Instagram.
- "Doesn't matter if you know how to solve a problem. If people don't know about you, it's all a moot point."
- He read Cashvertising, Ogilvy on Advertising and Russell Brunson's books on creating characters.
- He says getting attention is addicting, so you keep studying and writing.

chunks.heading: Be the niche of one
chunks.text:
- Competition worry: "There's a million of me", but he treats more people entering as validation, not competition.
- "I'm the brand, I'm the niche. The niche is me. And when the niche is me, I don't compete with anyone else."
- He tells people to be entertaining, humorous, funny or polarizing, so people want to follow them.
- He references Kevin Kelly's 1,000 true fans.
- His own example: he built a sales org at PatientPop from zero to 50 million. He could have said Mark Roberge (HubSpot, zero to 100 million) is "the expert", but many people struggle to reach a million and need someone closer to their stage.

chunks.heading: Starting on LinkedIn (late 2018)
chunks.text:
- He chose LinkedIn because a former report, Kevin Dorsey, was writing there as a sales thought leader.
- Twitter then looked like "news" to him, and he didn't want video or Instagram.
- He first tried a video series, long blog posts and mini webinars. Then one post got roughly 3-4 million impressions, and he committed to writing daily.
- LinkedIn is seen as a resume or jobs site, so writing there "like people use Twitter" made him stand out.
- His goal was to become a better writer. He treats it as a platform-agnostic practice: "you're just typing into a box and hitting send."
- He applied his sales-leader habits: analyze the data, double down on what works, cut what doesn't. He studied formatting, being compelling and being polarizing.

chunks.heading: Getting initial traction and post structure
chunks.text:
Two early levers:
- Comment under large accounts, with value, and be first.
- LinkedIn has no notification bell, so he suggests messaging 3-5 favorite thought leaders to ask when they post.
- He says this alone can take you from 1,000 to 10,000 followers.
- Publish consistently with a fixed structure.

His post framework:
- Write the meat first: what you want to teach (steps, like a Twitter thread).
- Then the hook: line 1 is the scroll stopper, line 2 is the validator, line 3 gets the click on "see more".
- End with a recap (a TLDR so people can join the conversation without rereading) and a call to conversation ("what would you add? agree, disagree?").

chunks.heading: Content system and cross-platform "suction"
chunks.text:
- He built a "content matrix": topics down the left, structures across the top (observations, step-by-step guides, how-tos, analytical, X vs Y, past vs present, listicles).
- Once a week (Saturday morning), he pairs topics with structures and writes about 10 headlines, then drafts about 10 pieces in 2 hours.
- Tools: Hypefury for scheduling and templates, Hemingway app for readability (clear, low grade level).
- He posts the same content to LinkedIn, Twitter, Instagram and his website.
- Audience at the time: about 130,000 LinkedIn followers and 50,000 newsletter subscribers.
- Suction trick: post an article on LinkedIn, share a snippet and redirect to Twitter. LinkedIn followers like the tweet, which exposes it to strangers.
- Result he cites: roughly 5 weeks on Twitter after he started, taking him to about 22,000 followers.
- His daily rhythm: post at 7:15 a.m. Central, then 45 minutes of engagement.

chunks.heading: Selling: organic reach, impulse-buy pricing, and the promotion flywheel
chunks.text:
- He has never run paid ads and doesn't know how. He'd consider them for a SaaS with strong lifetime value, and would hire someone to run them.
- His belief: a large organic following plus clear positioning sells more than ads.
- Pricing: "impulse buy" products. First product 50 dollars. Current product 150 dollars, often with a 25-30% discount. No 1,200 dollar masterclasses, because they need a lot of trust.
- He calls these "trust tripwires": a low-cost, high-value product that earns trust.
- Promotion steps:
  1. Prove expertise (every post gets 100,000 or more impressions).
  2. Show money results (screenshots of revenue from LinkedIn and products).
  3. Describe the outcome of a big following: job offers, podcast and stage invites, sales, awards.
  4. Name the gap, offer a "peek behind the curtain" (his copywriting friend Eddie Shlainer's "curtain language"), then state the price.
- Flywheel: buyers get a video-testimonial request 2 weeks later. He has about 2,500 students and hundreds of video testimonials, auto-fed to the landing page. Conversion rises as more testimonials arrive.
- He says everything in his paid product has been shared free somewhere. People pay for aggregation: everything in one place and getting from A to B in an hour.

chunks.heading: Private community and diversification
chunks.text:
- His private community costs 99 dollars per quarter, another impulse-buy price.
- He tried yearly first, but it hurt his optionality (stuck for 9 more months if he dislikes running it).
- Quarterly keeps people long enough to see value (about 90 days) and keeps him able to close in 3 months. He hasn't tested monthly.
- It gives him about 2,000 people to whom he can drop links for future products.
- He frames it as a diversified portfolio of income and distribution.

chunks.heading: Small bets, diversification and bios
chunks.text:
- Advice he thinks people skip: spread risk. "I'd rather build 10 50,000 dollar businesses than one 500,000 dollar business." He credits Daniel Vassallo's small-bets thinking.
- Pattern he describes: build a service business, productize it once understood, then build another.
- Vision: instead of product studios, a "distribution studio" where creators with large audiences bundle reach (he imagines collectively 500 million impressions a year) and take equity in products they launch.
- Platform-specific bios: LinkedIn says "one-person businesses" (solopreneur wording resonates); Twitter says "no-code businesses" because it is tech-heavy, and he wants to signal he's not an engineer.
- He now calls himself an entrepreneur, not a "personal brand": "a walking business," not a brand.

chunks.heading: Habits that support the business
chunks.text:
- Background: after about 10 years in high-growth SaaS (Zocdoc, PatientPop), he burned out. He says burnout is about loss of control, not hours worked.
- After a panic attack in December 2018, he stepped down and stayed about 8 more months. He quit alcohol for 90 days.
- With his wife he walked 10 miles a day (3 miles three times) and lost about 40 lb.
- Today's schedule: coffee with his wife from 6:00, post at 7:15, 45 minutes of engagement, walk or gym, about 90 minutes of writing daily.
- Tuesday to Thursday afternoons are for advising early-stage SMB SaaS clients. Monday and Friday are for business systems: eliminate, automate, delegate.
- He plans to test moving writing to the morning, when he's sharpest, and exercise to the afternoon.
- His principle: do more of what gives energy and less of what doesn't.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Justin Welsh explains how burnout led him to build a one-person business that hit $5M. He covers starting fast on one platform, turning audience questions into products, de-risking with diversified revenue, discovery-based selling, pricing courses low for trust, and building a movement.

chunks.heading: Why he left corporate and how he started
chunks.text:
- Justin spent 10 years in high-growth startups. He was an early sub-1 employee at Zocdoc in 2009 (5 years), then VP Sales and Chief Revenue Officer at PatientPop, where he grew the sales and marketing team from one person to 150 and revenue from the first dollar to $70M.
- On December 16, 2018 he had his first panic attack and called 911. He says that day made him know he needed to "do something different". Becoming a creator or starting a one-person business was not the plan.
- His burnout came from loss of control: problems stacked up faster than he could solve them, and everything became urgent and important. He coped with wine, burgers, 4 hours of sleep and weighed 240 lbs (about 210 now).
- He gave notice and took about 7 more months to leave so he could hand off his team. In that period he lost 40-50+ lbs.
- He planned to try working for himself for six months, then go back to a VP Sales or CRO job. He started on August 1, 2019.
- Burnout warning signs are hard to see because feeling bad becomes your normal. His fixes: journal daily (what is going well, poorly, what he is grateful for), build a business that supports your life, and have a peer group. He has Slack and Discord groups of people doing the same work.

chunks.heading: Life first, business second
chunks.text:
- His core principle is "Your life should come first, your business should come second." Build free time, breaks and reflection into the business.
- Step one is defining what you enjoy and what you want to avoid. You cannot cut every disliked task from day one, but you can plan to eliminate them over time.
- He calls his temptation "shiny outcome syndrome" (different from shiny object syndrome). He sees a peer like Hunter Hammond building many businesses, then lists the work required and decides "I don't want to do that." He then returns to the grounding question of how he wants his life to be.
- He wants growth only if it does not disrupt his life. A Slack community he launched two years earlier fit his lifestyle badly, and he regretted going against that judgment.
- His regimented day:
  - 6:00-8:30am: coffee and time with his wife, plus 30-45 minutes on social media with his audience.
  - Then a 5-7 mile walk or 90 minutes at the gym, nearly every day, with his wife.
  - About 3 hours of work at his peak, 1-4pm.
  - 4-5pm: open slot for meetings and calls.
  - Evenings free.
- He treats the creator job like a 9-to-5 so that freedom does not turn into drift.

chunks.heading: Choosing what to build on and getting started
chunks.text:
- His four-part framework for what you are good at:
  - Skills from your work experience.
  - What you are obsessed with and could talk about for hours.
  - What people ask you for help with.
  - What you have solved for yourself, since others behind you want the same fix.
- It does not need to be the right answer long-term. Five years in, he no longer talks about healthcare tech or SaaS, the topics he started with, and has pivoted three or four times.
- "Start then learn, don't learn then start" (he credits Sahil Lavingia). He bought one book, read it, and went to LinkedIn. He chose LinkedIn because he was afraid of Twitter and nobody there was treating it like Twitter.
- He wrote about what he had lived: building an SDR team, inbound marketing, working with the VP of marketing, setting up customer success.
- Pick the platform you will use daily, because "consistency and persistence are the two most important traits." If it fails, you have eliminated a third of the options.
- He picks "interesting" over "fun". If you pick something you are not interested in, the work is never fun and the foundation is off.
- You need real skill. "It pays to be good at something," so get good first and then show others how. Many creators have no big resume; the easiest route to an interesting online business is doing interesting things in real life.

chunks.heading: From content to first dollar: listen for the problem
chunks.text:
- Start by teaching: share what you have learned, the journey, mistakes and wins. If no audience gathers, improve the writing, podcasting or video rather than blaming the idea.
- Then talk to the people who reach out. Use DMs, comments and 10-minute calls to find the recurring problems.
- His first product came from this. He wrote about healthcare SaaS but kept getting asked how he got so much engagement on LinkedIn. He turned that into a 60-minute video called the LinkedIn Playbook, priced at $50 in 2019. It sold about $75K in 18 months, and he first made money while he slept.
- He says he might still be consulting for healthcare companies in 2023-24 if he had not made that choice.
- If you hear the same question 50 times, build a product or service for it even if you do not love it. The lessons transfer to what you care about more.
- "It's not Revenue, it's problems." Examples:
  - Students kept saying they still struggled with the same thing, so he added templates.
  - A big company wanted to own the newsletter sponsorship slot with no competitors, so he built a new, higher-priced package and signed his biggest partner.
- Match the format to the customer problem, not to what you want to do. If they need hand-holding, build a service. If they want to learn on their own, build a course. For monthly tips, use a subscription email. For exposure, use a partnership.

chunks.heading: Discovery calls and selling a service
chunks.text:
- There are two kinds of discovery: asking questions to make a sale, and asking because you are curious about the customer's problem. He prefers curiosity, with follow-ups like "why do you think that?" and "who did you hear it from?"
- Specificity wins. When he was a buyer at PatientPop, every SEO agency pitched generic "we do SEO for companies like yours", and he picked the one who described how healthcare SEO had changed.
- Structure of his solution call:
  - Recap the problem in their words: the drop, what they tried, what it costs, the personal toll, the deadline.
  - Reference similar clients and name the differences from their case.
  - Lay out the method in steps, with a checkpoint to test the direction.
  - Give a contingency plan if the checkpoint fails.
  - Give a timeline and cost against the money recovered. His example: recover about $85K for about $5K in about 65 days.
  - Ask for a longer commitment afterward, painting a "positive future" (for example, growing on three more platforms).
- The pricing test: a business exists if you can solve a $30,000 problem for $4,000.
- He dislikes feature dumps. Solve the one problem the person named instead of listing 30 features.
- Use the customer's own language for pains and for the positive future. He writes his content, copy and emails with words people have said to him.

chunks.heading: Courses and the trust tripwire
chunks.text:
- Courses have low friction to enter, like books, so he does not blame the medium.
- His "trust tripwire": pick a problem you are 100% sure you can solve, build the best solution on the market, and price it so low it feels like a steal.
  - His LinkedIn course is $150, has 17,000 students, and the most common feedback is that it should cost $1,500.
  - He argues someone who gets a huge return at $150 will trust him at $500 later. He is playing the long game against people selling $2,500 courses with no trust.
  - He captures testimonials with a frictionless process and puts thousands on his landing page. More testimonials raise conversion, which brings more students and more word of mouth. He has 23,000 students and about a 4.98 rating.
- Teach simply. He explained LinkedIn to an 81-year-old friend and uses a "teach a fourth grader" approach. His wife dislikes social media, so he tests courses on her. When she is confused, he finds the step where it breaks.
- Test on people outside your audience. If a newcomer follows a 30-minute video, it works.
- Pre-sell before building. Early courses were sold before they were made. His example of validation: talk about the topic, then offer a pre-sale at $99 against $400 later. If it makes $50K, build it. If not, refund. His newest course had a 16,000-person waitlist, so he built it first.
- He says questions about landing page tools, launch timing or exact follower counts matter less than basics. The basics are find a problem, understand it deeply, learn how to solve it, show you can, build the product or service, and paint a positive future.

chunks.heading: Reducing risk: one audience, many revenue streams
chunks.text:
- He admits he worries daily that revenue could vanish (he was fired from his first three jobs). He de-risks by diversifying within one audience.
- The sequence he recommends:
  - Start with a service business using your skill. It is the fastest way to backfill a salary.
  - Quit your job only after 6-9 months of side income at roughly 60-70% of take-home pay and trending flat or up. Ask whether 40 more hours a week could get you to 100%.
  - Niche the service to the customers you love and who love you, then raise rates. Work less for the same money and use the time to build a digital product for people outside your ideal customer profile.
  - Add a newsletter with sponsorships once you have a large following. His example: 50-60K followers could grow a list to 10-15K subscribers, and at $1,000 per issue weekly that is $52K a year.
  - Add narrow, cheap upsells. His monthly templates are 5 social media templates for $9 a month, with 3,000 subscribers, about $27,000 a month, from one email sent.
- His public claim: $5 million in revenue in 1,548 days with no ads and a 92% margin. The tweet says "my little one-person business crossed $5 million".
- He is clear he is an outlier. Of 23,000 students, he knows of 3 who built $1-2M businesses and at least 100 emails from people making $80-100K. He does not promise "be the next me" and presents solopreneurship as an option, not the only path.

chunks.heading: Scaling and building a movement
chunks.text:
- Getting from $100K to a million: "You do the thing that got you to $100,000 longer." Revenue has grown with followers, impressions and subscribers, and it is a marathon where most people quit.
- Other levers: eliminate what does not work, automate, outsource what you lack time for, focus on creative work, and understand customer lifetime value and cost to acquire so you know how to spend $1 to make $3.
- Three things to get right: build a movement, use emotional language about people's desired future, and outlast competitors.
- His movement is "life first, business second", which he has talked about since October 2021, and the one-person creator movement. People who buy into a movement are more likely to buy products that get them there, and he hopes for customers for life.
- Movements need an enemy, and it does not have to be a person. His enemy is "living a life of regret". He cites Nike as a commodity turned movement, and credits Russell Brunson for the idea of a common enemy to "throw rocks at".
- Pain is useful. Asked what he would tell his 2018 self, he says he would not wish it away: "you're about to experience something very life-changing, lean into it."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Justin Welsh explains how he moved from SaaS advising to a solopreneur course and newsletter business. He covers quitting gradually, using customer feedback to choose products, pricing and positioning, and why slow, trust-based growth beats hacks. He also shares how he uses AI as a sounding board rather than a writer.

chunks.heading: Audience data and the feedback loop behind his products
chunks.text:
- Justin's audience data: 79.9% (roughly 8 in 10) either haven't started a business or run something part-time that doesn't make enough money.
- He concludes beginners don't need inspiration or "pie in the sky strategy." They need "what button do I press" and "what time do I do this thing" level instructions.
- His Saturday Solopreneur newsletter (101 issues at the time) is built for this: tactical and actionable, readable in under 4 minutes (about 250 seconds).
- He found most business newsletters were 15-minute philosophical reads with little tactical content.
- Every reader suggestion is a potential issue. After 101 issues he had roughly 1,000 feedback data points, which he bundled into the Creator MBA course.
