- Many people think they aren't experts. He calls this "knowledge blindness." His test: your high school math teacher isn't Einstein, just ahead of the students. Don't compare yourself to Gary Vaynerchuk.
- "Create content for the you from two to three years ago." You only need to be ahead of the people you teach.

chunks.heading: Three ways to build a relevant tribe
chunks.text:
- **Be a leader.** Share what you've already done. Ask: where was I 2-3 years ago, are there people there now, and can I get them where I am faster with fewer mistakes? Most of his own content is this.
- **Discover and curate.** If you lack expertise, do the research for your audience and package it. Example: Sumit Garg on Twitter breaks down Bezos's shareholder letters, Apple letters and mental models, and has about 40,000 followers at 22.
- **Interview and distribute.** Interview experts in your sub-niche and share the findings. Example: Chris Fladzook, a Yale senior, interviews famous founders through the entrepreneurs club and gets heavy engagement despite no tech experience.
- You can mix all three and test which your audience likes most.

chunks.heading: Inbound lead funnel: from LinkedIn to email
chunks.text:
Justin wants to move people off LinkedIn because the algorithm can change any time. He wants a place where he controls the narrative and communication.

1. **Daily post.** Each morning he writes one post, hoping readers click through to his profile.
2. **Featured section with two links.** "TOF" (top of funnel) is a free LinkedIn advice article for people not ready to buy. "BOF" (bottom of funnel) is his course for ready buyers.
3. **Evergreen article for email.** A big, robust guide you update over time (still valuable in 5-10 years). Readers trade their email address for it, which opts them into his weekly newsletter.
4. **Automated emails.** Consistency matters, so weekly or bi-weekly (he usually writes once a week). He teaches using two or three offers to sell product, service or business. Each morning 50-60 people receive an email from him, and one or two buy. He calls it an automated machine that "takes some time" to build.

chunks.heading: Outbound leads with Google Alerts
chunks.text:
His two-step outbound method needs only automation and no sales pitch.

1. Set up Google Alerts for ideal prospects. In his health-tech days, he alerted on every healthcare company raising a Series A (a company with fresh money to spend).
2. Save the alerts and, every Friday at 9am, message the CEOs who raised money, about 50 people a week.

- The message is only congratulations: no pitch, no PDF, no "here's why to pay attention to me." Example: "congrats on the round, I'm a healthcare technology veteran, love what you're doing, following you from Los Angeles."
- Replies led to calls and customers. He named Swell ($2.5M seed) and Okadak ($10M Series A) as examples that became customers.
- He usually lands a handful of customers from this.

chunks.heading: His story, results, and the course offer
chunks.text:
- Background: about 12 years in high-growth tech. He was the tenth employee at Zocdoc (2009-2014; about 10 to roughly 1,000 employees, valued at $2 billion). He was then CRO and senior VP of sales at PatientPop in LA, growing from no money to over $50M in recurring revenue in four and a half years.
- In late 2018 he had a panic attack serious enough for an ambulance. He weighed 240 lbs (now 190), told his CEO in January 2019 he was burning out, and stepped down in August 2019.
- He chose LinkedIn deliberately: he disliked Twitter, didn't want to be on video, and wasn't going to do photos for Instagram. He saw that almost nobody used LinkedIn like social media: "an untapped goldmine."
- Results as of August 2021: about 115,000 followers, five revenue streams run through LinkedIn (advising, consulting, coaching, a private community called Audience and Income, digital products), over $1M with zero paid ads. He says he has helped 3,000 people start side hustles. His wife Jennifer grew from 2,500 to 40,000 followers in six months using his method.
- Warning: "There are no get-rich-quick schemes." Building an audience is "not fast, not passive, not overnight."
- Advice on working while employed: he told his co-CEOs he'd write from 7:15 to 8:15am and asked if that was a problem. He recommends getting your boss's permission, though he says you own your social accounts.
- Outcomes drive content: identify your goal (consulting business, promotion, new job, speaking) and niche from there. His own advising serves only early-stage, transactional SaaS companies in healthcare technology.
- Course: "The Operating System," launched 30 days earlier with 1,200 students and a perfect five-star rating. Two hours, 30+ lessons, normally $250, offered here at $150 (he said he was about to raise the price). Includes a swipe file, sub-niche playbook and backstory builder, with a 30-day refund policy and only one or two refunds so far.
- He answers DMs poorly (about 100 a day), so he suggests connecting and commenting publicly.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Justin explains how he built a Notion-based content operating system that turns one newsletter into 28 weekly pieces, why he shut down a profitable paid community, and how LinkedIn and Twitter differ. Core lessons: systematize away friction, price for optionality, and optimize for money rather than impressions.

chunks.heading: How Justin builds a content operating system for a one-person business
chunks.text:
- Justin's business runs on content: more content pushed out means more top-of-funnel followers on Twitter and LinkedIn and more newsletter growth.
- He has no employees. His virtual assistant only handles admin, customer service and support, so he is "forced to have systems."
- His background is executive SaaS: two $50M ARR companies, teams of 150+ and $300M+ in venture capital raised. Process at that scale made systems "second nature."
- Weekly output he has to produce:
  - 1 newsletter
  - 10 LinkedIn posts
  - 10 Twitter posts
  - 1 Twitter thread
  - 1 LinkedIn carousel
  - 6 LinkedIn business-account posts
  - That is 28 pieces of content in total.
- He starts by listing the outputs, then arranges them in the order that makes sense to him.

chunks.heading: Hub-and-spoke: the newsletter first, everything else derived from it
chunks.text:
- Many creators write short social posts, see what resonates, then turn that into a newsletter. That did not work for Justin. He finds the newsletter the hardest piece, so he moves it to the front of the week.
- The newsletter goes out Saturday and he aims to finish it Monday. It is the "hub" of the system.
- The other roughly 20 short-form posts come from the newsletter, which he pushes through "six to ten different lenses":
  - story
  - observation
  - contrarian take
  - listicle
  - past versus present
  - present versus future
  - analysis
  - teardown
- His line: learn to "say the same thing a thousand different ways." This also serves audiences who learn differently, since some like motivational stories and others like step-by-step guides.
- Twitter thread: copy the newsletter text, chunk it, add headers and subheaders.
- LinkedIn carousel: take the same thread, chop it up into a PDF, and post it on LinkedIn. It is the same content in a different format on a different platform.

chunks.heading: Building the system by removing friction
chunks.text:
- Justin's rule: any time he hits friction, he asks how to systematize removing it. The system grows from each snag.
- Evolution of the weekly process:
  - Version one was just "newsletter, then content."
  - First Monday: he sat down and had no topic. Fix: an ideation step. Tuesday and Thursday he sets aside 30 minutes to ideate, by watching favorite creators' YouTube channels and most popular videos, scanning newsletters (including Josh's) for a topic he can add his take to, and checking his RSS feeds and Readwise.
  - Next: the newsletter needed more than opinion, so he added a research step.
  - Next: he forgot to edit, so he added an editing step with a short list of questions to run through.
- The end result is a roughly 10-step process built in Notion. Each Monday he opens step one and works through the instructions, producing a newsletter, two pieces of promotional content, 20 short-form posts, a thread, a carousel and six business posts.
- He calls it the "content operating system" and sells it as a course (an eight-step process).
- "When I don't feel motivated, creative, excited, that's where systems come in."
- Justin agrees that a good system is about formats, not topics. It works regardless of subject, and it evolves rather than being finished.
- On the objection that systems kill authenticity: his Twitter feed looks different every day because the lenses vary. Movies, music and every creative profession follow templates, and audiences don't notice.

chunks.heading: Why Justin shut down his paid community
chunks.text:
- The community was a Slack-based paid membership. It was thriving at about $14k MRR, members loved it and were resubscribing. He shut it down anyway, as a lifestyle choice.
- Two things make a community work, in his view:
  - Goal alignment: it is not "the Justin Welsh community" but a community of creators and solopreneurs who all want one-person businesses and are aiming at the same target.
  - Shared context: members have been through a similar journey, such as the same self-paced course or cohort-based program, so they share the same jargon. He got the first right but did not build the second (putting people who had completed a specific program together).
- Why he closed it:
  - A commitment "drastically reduces optionality." Selling annual memberships tethered him to a 12-month commitment.
  - He wanted time for more courses, a book, possibly a cohort-based coaching program and a micro SaaS.
  - His personality didn't suit a synchronous community. Because it always existed on Slack, a free block of time (e.g. noon to three) was never really free. With members in 61 countries, someone was always awake, so "you never had a day off."
- On whether people came for him or for each other: he admits he was probably part of the draw. What keeps people in a community is connecting them with one other meaningful person.
- He gave members a 90-day notice so as not to pull the rug out. He told members they could start their own community as long as it wasn't tied to his name or brand and didn't solicit from his community.
- He warns that running one involves a lot of customer service (logins, tech issues), so leaving it open and free would still have been a near full-time support role.

chunks.heading: Pricing a membership community: quarterly beats monthly or annual
chunks.text:
- He began with annual plans and enrolled three cohorts. Each cohort extended his commitment another 12 months, and he did not want to shut down and refund people.
- He moved to quarterly memberships and calls that "the sweet spot," the model he would use if he ran a community again.
- Reasoning:
  - Monthly lets people "kick tires for two seconds and then exit." He didn't want to build "that hotel environment."
  - Annual, from the creator's side, "drastically reduces that optionality."
  - Quarterly keeps him always 90 days away from stopping, while committing members long enough to learn the channels, attend events, make friends and get entrenched.

chunks.heading: LinkedIn versus Twitter: different content, same mechanics
chunks.text:
- Both platforms have creators, consumers and a feed. Justin went LinkedIn to Twitter; he sees many Twitter creators doing the reverse.
- LinkedIn:
  - Highly professional. People are there to learn how to get better at their job.
  - Content that works is practical, tactical, emotional, inspirational and story-driven.
  - Pithy, ironic or philosophical one-liners (Naval-style) do not play well there.
  - 3,000 characters, and posts are truncated with a "see more" break. Writing long-form on LinkedIn is like writing a thread every day, so he teases the rest with hook lines at the top.
- Twitter (in his echo chamber):
  - Leans interesting, philosophical and unique; you have to be unique and interesting to stand out.
  - 280 characters.
- LinkedIn to Twitter: compress. He took his LinkedIn content and made it short, bulleted, with lots of white space and short sentences, and it did well.
- Twitter to LinkedIn: move threads into a LinkedIn post (educational, step-by-step content works), and bring over popular tweets. Keep it professional and tight; there is not much trolling on LinkedIn.
- LinkedIn is consumer-heavy, with everyone consuming, which is why he calls it so valuable for audience, income and business growth. He saw the opportunity in 2019 and says there was "a lot of luck."
- Repurposing a short tweet on LinkedIn: if both the brevity and the idea made it popular, keep it short. If it was the idea, expand it with extra information and a call to action or call to conversation. He often posts a 280-character piece on LinkedIn, then again three months later with content added, checks the results in Shield Analytics, and stores it for a six-month repurpose. The answer comes from the data.

chunks.heading: Putting links in LinkedIn posts
chunks.text:
- The common advice is not to link in posts because it hurts impressions, and he agrees it does: his average post gets about 150,000 impressions and a post with a link gets about 70k, roughly a 50% reduction.
- But click-through rate is about 7x higher than telling people to "find it in my featured section" or spelling out a URL, which he says kills clicks.
- His reasoning: "My business doesn't run on impressions, my business runs on money." Because so few people do it, he stands out.
- He links in the post itself (not the comments) on about 5 of his 10-12 weekly LinkedIn posts, nearly half.
- The link is never an aggressive ask. Process:
  - Write a newsletter on a topic such as building an online course, then push it through the lenses.
  - Write an educational, relatively long story post, since the further a reader gets, the more likely they are to act.
  - At the bottom, offer a free guide or the newsletter issue on his site.
  - That drives about 4,000 people a day to the newsletter issue on his website. At the bottom of the issue he passively lists three ways he can help (courses and services).
- Example he gave: the morning's post had 4,000 engagements, the afternoon's was heading toward 700, and he had more website traffic right then than that morning.

chunks.heading: Choosing and sequencing platforms
chunks.text:
- Pick based on where the audience plays.
  - LinkedIn: coaches in B2B SaaS, sales development, marketing, customer success, executive leadership, i.e. professionals trying to do better at their job.
  - Twitter: niche or hobby topics such as health and fitness, trainers, crypto.
- Use a tool like SparkToro to find where an audience actually hangs out. Both platforms are excellent for building businesses.
- Start with one platform. Most people start with too many and underestimate how long it takes. He agrees you grow faster focused on one.
- His own timeline:
  - Three years on LinkedIn (about two and a half years of daily posting) and he built 200,000+ followers before posting his first week of Twitter content.
  - On Twitter since 2009, but began posting daily on October 25th (the prior year).
- His offers (mentioned by name): LinkedIn Operating System (grow and monetize a LinkedIn account) and Content Operating System (the eight-step process above), both at justinwelsh.me.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Justin explains how he built a solo content system: start with a 30-minute daily habit, add structure each time friction appears, and write one newsletter that gets chopped into many social posts. He also covers niching down and low-friction pricing that follows discovery then trust.

chunks.heading: Building a content system: start with one daily habit and add structure as friction appears
chunks.text:
- Justin says there is no single right system, and his own is just one version.
- To start, he'd make a system out of producing one piece of content a day. Most people "read a lot, study a lot, research a lot" and call it "procrastination dressed up as action."
- Simplest system: block 30 minutes on the calendar every day for content.
- Each time you hit the block, new friction shows up, and you add one thing to remove it:
  - Don't know what to write: add prompting questions ("did I learn anything today?", "did I help someone?", "what do people ask me?").
  - Can't get it into a good format: add format templates, such as listicle templates.
- The system grows iteratively, and after four years his is close to automated and runs faster each time.
- His system exists because he is forced to do everything himself. He has no employees and no ghostwriter. His only helper is a virtual assistant who handles customer service and support tickets, with no content work.
- His output includes a weekly newsletter, 12 LinkedIn pieces, 12 tweets, a Twitter thread, and events like this one. Without a system he would burn out, as he did at PatientPop.

chunks.heading: Hub-and-spoke: one newsletter as the pillar, chopped into 5-7 pieces of short-form content
chunks.text:
- Ideation is the starting point of all content. Set aside 15-30 minutes a day to brain dump ideas, however good or bad. He keeps a running Notion page with 150+ ideas.
- Two ways to run the flow:
  - Short form first: turn one idea into several posts, see which resonate, then extend the winner into a newsletter, blog or guide. The posts act as small tests in the field.
  - Justin's way, the opposite: ideate, write the newsletter, then chop the newsletter into 5-7 pieces.
- Result: he always has one pillar piece (the newsletter) plus outlying posts that all point back to it.
- Social posts can say "if you want to learn more, go to my newsletter." That moves thousands of people off social platforms onto his website, where they can subscribe, buy a course, sign up for coaching, sponsor the newsletter, or learn more about him.
- One idea can become many angles. Example idea "four fastest ways to grow a YouTube channel" becomes:
  - a story about someone who grew a channel
  - an observation about five channels you watch
  - eight tools top channels use
  - a present vs. future take (how creators will work in 2027)
  - the most uncommon channels that are growing fast
- Same lenses on a newsletter about LinkedIn copywriting: a story, an observation, a listicle (top eight LinkedIn copywriters), a contrarian take (why a popular formula doesn't work on LinkedIn), present vs. future.

chunks.heading: His weekly workflow: ideate, research, write with a template, edit, chop, distribute
chunks.text:
1. **Ideate.** Two 30-minute blocks a week. Aim for 6-10 unique ideas a week while needing only one, so the bank keeps growing. He picks the idea Monday morning. Sources:
   - favorite YouTubers' channels sorted by most popular (popular videos signal topics people care about)
   - curated newsletters in his inbox, e.g. a piece on getting your first 5,000 Twitter followers prompts "my own spin" on it, not a copy
2. **Research.** Google, advanced Twitter search and LinkedIn search for a quote, article, book, tweet or post that backs up or adds context to his point. He also looks for contrarian takes.
3. **Write the newsletter through the same template every week.** Writing a newsletter is hard and most people quit, so templates are the fix. His structure: introduce a problem, why it matters, how most people try to solve it, why that's wrong, then how he would solve it.
4. **Edit with a checklist of questions.** Is it clear and concise? Does it deliver on the headline's promise? Is everything linked? Are there illustrations? Is it easy to read? Any rambling run-on sentences?
5. **Chop and distribute.** Push the finished newsletter through the lenses above to make posts for LinkedIn and Twitter.

He summarizes the system as "ideation, research, writing, editing, chopping and distributing."

chunks.heading: Newsletter copywriting formula: Pain, Amplification, Intrigue, Positive future, Solution
chunks.text:
- Justin uses a formula he made up, a take on Pain-Agitate-Solution. He calls it Pain, Amplification, Intrigue, Positive Future, Solution.
- Steps:
  - **Pain:** state a problem his audience has. He knows them because after four years in the space, readers tell him. Example: you spend an hour on a post, 30 minutes editing, then hit publish and get "crickets."
  - **Amplification:** twist the knife and make it existential. You miss podcast invites, can't build your business, can't drive your career forward, can't get attention.
  - **Intrigue:** set up the content, e.g. "what if I told you there were five tips most people don't use on LinkedIn to write faster, better, more predictably and at scale?"
  - **Positive future:** describe the outcome, e.g. content in 10 minutes, 5x engagement, new opportunities, a podcast appearance, your first business.
  - **Solution:** "here's how I would do it."
- Rationale: it takes the reader top to bottom through human psychology and emotion. Most of his writing is "psychological" rather than just putting ideas on paper and hoping they're interesting.
- Topics stay on one theme, building a one-person business, with subtopics: audience growth, efficiency and productivity, monetization, products and services.

chunks.heading: Writing for each platform: study why you stop scrolling, then obsess over the opening
chunks.text:
- Never copy-paste a newsletter into social posts. Reformat for each platform.
- His first trick is being cognizant. When he scrolls Twitter or LinkedIn, he asks why he stopped before reading the post. Was it the first line, a word in the second line, a number, a big number, a combination?
- Second, understand how people make decisions:
  - **Twitter thread:** mostly the opening tweet matters. If it's strong, people commit to the rest.
  - **LinkedIn:** the lines above the "see more" fold matter most. A click on "see more" is a commitment to read.
- His formula for LinkedIn posts:
  - a first line that "punches you in the face" (he credits Sean Perry)
  - empathy or context in the second line
  - a hook line before the see more, teased "like a radio teaser" to get the click
- Emotion drives sharing: belonging, pain, education, entertainment, empathy.
  - Personal-life platitudes (for example, a restaurant's egg sandwich) don't interest people as much as you think.
  - He aims to elicit a positive or sometimes polarizing reaction, not to be "divisive, cruel, angry, nasty." The aim is to make people think. "No one's ever going to like you" across the whole crowd, so say something you believe with intention.

chunks.heading: Choosing a niche: start tight, be "the only," and bring a non-obvious solution
chunks.text:
- Start with the smallest, tightest niche, where you can become an expert and resonate deeply with a smaller audience. Then add larger concentric circles around it as you grow. Justin says Monday leadership, Tuesday fintech, Wednesday government never gains traction.
- Example: don't say "I help small businesses grow." Say you work with flower shops doing six figures to take them past seven figures with email marketing. You are then probably the only person in that niche and have no competition.
- Two steps:
  1. Niche down so you're the only, or one of 5-10, people in the space.
  2. Bring a non-obvious solution to an obvious problem. Agencies that all pitch "Facebook ads for SaaS companies" are commodities that race to the bottom on price. He cites Chris Walker, who talks about "dark social" and argues marketing teams are doing it wrong.
- Justin's own path: entrepreneur, then solopreneur (one person, no employees), then diversified solopreneur. He is building five revenue streams toward $5 million in recurring revenue, a very specific phrase and goal. He says that on that path he is one of a very few options for people who want it.
- Once you've built an audience, you can bring in more interests. Fans who followed you for one reason will follow you into others. Be patient: start with one and expand.
- He keeps his craft-beer interest off LinkedIn.

chunks.heading: From discovery to trust to impulse buy; engagement pods and growth
chunks.text:
- Justin says he rarely makes a traditional "ask." He thinks of the path as awareness, then trust, then purchase:
  - **Discovery:** two tweets and two LinkedIn posts a day.
  - **Trust:** the longer-form newsletter, free guides, articles and blog posts, which move people from social platforms to his website where they see how he thinks.
  - **Purchase:** priced as an impulse buy. He has no $2,000 masterclass or $4,997 coaching program. He sells $150 courses.
- He positions products "very passively": if you have one of these three problems, grab one of these courses for $150.
- Distribution: be where the audience is. His newsletter is on the web and by email, and he plans to add it as a LinkedIn newsletter (he has about 50,000 LinkedIn newsletter subscribers). He doesn't force email signups.
- Newsletter growth: 53,000 subscribers 10 months after launch. Many people read each Saturday on the website and never give an email, and he's fine with that.
- He is considering a podcast that reads the newsletter with extra context, since some people prefer to listen. Format audiences overlap less than people expect.
- Repetition: he has explained this content system about 30 times, yet people still say they've never seen it. People forget what you posted; his wife didn't remember a post she saw a year earlier.
- Engagement pods:
  - Justin reached 300,000 LinkedIn followers and about 70,000 Twitter followers without ever joining one.
  - He declines "trade a like for a like" requests.
  - He builds real relationships instead. Example: he and Austin Belsack met on LinkedIn four years ago, traded ebooks, recommendations and client introductions, and now support each other's content. "He's my friend."
  - Pod audiences are false engagement, not the right customers.

chunks.heading: Differentiating a local service business and running a company page
chunks.text:
- For small businesses in a small town, Justin says to look at your four or five largest competitors, who probably all use similar messaging, features and benefits. Instead:
  - Create "existential pain" and show you understand the prospect's problems better than competitors do, so they say "you must be in my head."
  - Say what competitors will recommend (A, B, C and D) and explain why you don't think those are best. Frame it as the game changing.
  - Present a different process, such as a custom audit that leads to a custom strategy.
  - Then quote prices and propose a next step.
- He says nobody cares that you're cheaper or have been around longer. "They care that you can solve their problems."
- On LinkedIn company pages, Justin says to be an industry expert and an incredible resource, not a pitch for your offering. Shine a light on other people in the industry so they give the page love in return. A personal page can add opinions and step-by-step teaching "two to three steps behind you on the journey."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Justin Welsh walks through the 23 steps from posting daily on LinkedIn to $10M in total revenue, with no paid ads and no employees. The path runs from noise to signal, a high-touch service business, a cheap trust-building product, then audience, community, newsletter, sponsorships and a flagship launch.

chunks.heading: Justin's path to $10M: timeline, channels and margins
chunks.text:
- Passed $10M in total revenue after 5 years and 9 months, built solo with no paid ads and no employees.
- Milestones: 29 months to the first $1M, then 9 months to $2M, 6 to $3M, 5 to $4M, 4 to $5M and $6M (same week), 3 to $7M, 3 to $8M, 5 to $9M, 6 to $10M.
- Channels were 100% organic: LinkedIn, X/Twitter, Instagram, his newsletter and SEO.
- Profit margin is about 89% today, down from about 99% at the start, because he added software, outsourced some work (website redesign, personalization/segmentation) and travels for work.
- He argues 90% margins "aren't attainable in nearly any other type of business" but are realistic for a solopreneur.
- Current revenue mix:
  - Products: $6.75M
  - Consulting: $1.17M
  - Sponsorships: $795k
  - Subscriptions: $695k
  - Community: $630k
- Team: his wife helps a lot, an outsourced VA answers support tickets, and he partners with people when needed (e.g. Brennan Dunn). He no longer does anything SaaS-related.
- He says the path isn't a template ("you may not have the same luck or timing") and that he is an outlier. It took six years and 5K+ pieces of content.
- His long-game advice: start a side project, build it to 60-70% of your salary, then go all in.

chunks.heading: Steps 1-6: Content, signal, a service business and a niche
chunks.text:
- **Create noise.** He wrote content daily before he had a business, just to find his voice. He began on LinkedIn about building a SaaS unicorn as CRO, with no strategy. The key is volume, not perfection.
- **Find the signal.** He tracked engagement metrics (comments, shares, DMs with questions), not vanity metrics, and doubled down on what resonated. He built a daily LinkedIn system that grew him from 2,000 to over 750,000 followers. At this point he had about 15,000.
- **Start with a service business.** Founders DM'd him about SaaS, he answered every DM, and then offered consulting. He argues your first business should be a high-touch, high-value service: you learn the market from customers and get immediate cash flow.
- **Find your ideal customer.** Look for the sweet spot between customers you love and those who love you. His was early-stage SMB SaaS founders in healthcare. "The riches are in the niches", and you can't niche down until you know who you serve best.
- **Double your rates.** With a niche, happy customers and testimonials, he doubled his rates, wrote content aimed at that niche and declined work outside it. Loop: higher rates = better clients = better results = even higher rates.
- **Reduce your time.** Instead of earning twice as much, he worked half the time for the same income and used the freed time to build more automated income. His rule: optimize for time, not just money.

chunks.heading: Steps 7-12: Productizing and pricing the first course
chunks.text:
- **Listen to your inbox.** Rereading LinkedIn DMs to find problems to productize, he found repetitive questions about SaaS sales and many about LinkedIn itself. "Your customers will tell you what to build next."
- **Test cheaply.** At 21K+ followers, people asked how he grew. He made a short course, *The LinkedIn Playbook*, sold at $50 and promoted with posts. It was casual, with no high production value. Don't overthink the first product.
- **First sales.** Listed on Gumroad on April 16, 2020, it made $10,482 in the first month. It was a different niche than his consulting, which confused him; his advice is to follow what customers will pay for.
- **Run with what works.** Over the next 15 months the Playbook brought in $75K. He kept consulting through VC networking, events like SaaStr and guest posts on other consultants' blogs. He says to run in two directions if you must; experiments show the path.
- **Raise price after building trust.** He rebuilt it as *The LinkedIn Operating System* with a 3x-4x price increase. The $50 price was his "trust tripwire": charge $50, deliver 100x the value, build a loyal base, then raise prices as you deliver results. Customers should press play and see results within days.
- **Align content and product.** With 100% of his LinkedIn content on audience growth and a product directly tied to it, the second version grossed $186K in 3 months, versus $75K in 15 months for the first. "When you go 'all in' in one direction, revenue explodes."

chunks.heading: Steps 13-15: Affiliates and the community he closed
chunks.text:
- **Affiliate army.** Halfway through the course, students are prompted to leave a testimonial and join the affiliate program, and the same automation runs at the end. Result: 3,247 affiliates generating $600K in revenue. "Your best customers can be your best marketers."
- **Community.** Selling about $2K/day in info products, his interest in consulting faded. He opened a private creator community at $199 per year, with course completers prompted to join.
- **Closing it.** It was a $15K MRR business, but he felt he had to be on Slack 24/7. After 15 months he shut it down. His takeaway: communities require constant attention, and "Sometimes the right business decision can feel wrong." Trust your instincts about the life you want.

chunks.heading: Steps 16-19: New channel, second course, MRR and newsletter
chunks.text:
- **Twitter.** With the freed time he started writing on X and reached 480K followers in under 2.5 years, reusing his LinkedIn growth know-how.
- **Second course.** While on a podcast with Dickie Bush and Nicolas Cole, their audience was struck by his simple content process. That led to *The Content Operating System*. His rule: your audience tells you what they want to learn next.
- **Monthly Templates.** He was making content templates for himself each week, so he tested them as a $9 upsell on each course. After 8 months it had 2,584 subscribers and $23.2K MRR. "The best products solve problems you're already solving for yourself."
- **Newsletter.** With 10,000+ students and template subscribers he wasn't emailing, he launched *The Saturday Solopreneur* in January 2022: one actionable idea each Saturday, readable in 4 minutes. It reached 185K subscribers in 40 months while he prunes the list regularly. "Consistency matters more than perfection."

chunks.heading: Steps 20-22: Sponsorships and the Creator MBA launch
chunks.text:
- **Sponsorships.** With 175K+ readers, he sells two slots per issue at $2,500 each, or $5,000 per weekly issue. Sponsors like Kajabi, Stan, Circle, Delphi and Taplio have booked 12x-15x each. Principle: build the audience first, monetize second.
- **Flagship product.** In 2023 he started *The Creator MBA*: 111 lessons, 19 hours of video, plus a 14-step framework you can watch in 2 hours to have your first business. He says a flagship "should be your best work. Don't rush it."
- **Personalized launch.** He brought in Brennan Dunn, an expert in personalized online product launches. This delayed release about six months. They built an 18-week personalized launch plan.
- **Result.** Launched January 16, 2024, it sold $1.6M in six days. His lesson: "The work happens before the launch, not during."

chunks.heading: Step 23: Unsubscribe Substack and membership
chunks.text:
- Nearing $10M, he wanted to write creatively and missed person-to-person connection, so he started a Substack called *Unsubscribe* and launched a membership alongside it.
- The Unsubscribe Membership includes real-time chat, a live weekly Q&A, monthly workshops and in-person networking events.
- It became a $19K MRR business in about one month.
- His principle: never stop experimenting, since the best businesses evolve with your interests.
- Closing principles: pay attention to signals, follow the paid customers, build what people need, and stay consistent.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Justin shares five lessons from his digital course business: building in public, accessible pricing that fuels word-of-mouth, testimonials as the best promotion, an 80/20 give/ask content ratio, and short courses that people finish. Each lesson is backed by his own revenue, conversion and completion numbers.

chunks.heading: Lesson 1: Building in public lifted conversion 2.7x and daily revenue about 8x
chunks.text:
- Justin built his first course, The LinkedIn Playbook, quietly at home. It made $11,781 in its first month, about $380 per day.
- He built the updated version, The LinkedIn Operating System (released July 2021), completely in public. He shared each day's wins, losses, metrics and revenue.
- It took 91 days to build and made $94,651 in the first month, about $3,053 per day.
- Both products got roughly the same landing page views. The public build converted 2.7x higher, even at 3x the price, partly because people could see what he was building and were invested in the journey.

chunks.heading: Lesson 2: Price for accessibility to create word-of-mouth
chunks.text:
- Justin notes creators with much smaller audiences selling a "masterclass" for $1,499. He thinks the trust and nurturing needed to close a deal like that is "pretty massive".
- His approach: price products affordably, make them as valuable as possible, and ask buyers to tell their friends if they enjoyed them.
- The result is a word-of-mouth affiliate engine. He has paid out over $138,000 in affiliate commission to generate $395,200 in sales.
- His rule of thumb: "It's easy to recommend a $150 product to your friends. $1,499? Not so much."
- He recommends pricing to be accessible so word-of-mouth does the distribution work.

chunks.heading: Lesson 3: Weekly testimonials are his strongest promotion
chunks.text:
- Customer words convert prospects at a much higher rate than the creator's own words.
- Once per week he shares a simple testimonial or a DM from a happy customer. Course sales go up about 2x to 3x on those days.
- A normal day does $3,500 to $4,500 in course sales. A testimonial day often does $10,000 or more.
- He calls this the most effective promotion he has, and it is "extremely passive".
- Organic word-of-mouth compounds it: someone is talking about The LinkedIn Operating System online every single day, across 17,000+ customers.
- His advice: treat every testimonial as a chance to convert more prospects, and share them.

chunks.heading: Lesson 4: Keep an 80/20 give-to-ask ratio
chunks.text:
- Justin creates about 50 pieces of content per month on LinkedIn and 55 on Twitter, 105 in total.
- He shares a testimonial about 8 to 10 times out of those 105, so he promotes less than 10% of the time.
- Weekly promotion therefore isn't excessive in the context of the whole content stream.
- His golden rule: give value 80% of the time or more, and promote 20% of the time or less.

chunks.heading: Lesson 5: Shorter courses get finished
chunks.text:
- The LinkedIn Playbook runs about 75 minutes and had a 45% completion rate. He cites the average for course creators as 13.8%.
- Idea.Audience.Proof.Product runs 3.5 hours and had roughly a 25% completion rate. He didn't promote it much.
- He believes the longer course was the better, more helpful one, but that doesn't matter if people don't finish it. In hindsight he would have made it much shorter.
- He thinks the longer you've been in the creator space and the more well-known you are, the longer and more robust your courses can be.
- For beginners: teach people what they want to learn in 45 minutes or less to increase completion and adoption.

chunks.heading: Summary and takeaway
chunks.text:
- His five lessons: build in public, price for accessibility, use testimonials, keep an 80/20 give/ask ratio, and keep courses short.
- His closing point: none of the lessons matter if you never get started.
- Headline figure behind the advice: over $3,000,000 in digital course sales (the essay title says $3,394,480).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Justin Welsh shares a three-step writing process behind his LinkedIn growth. He writes the informational "meat" first, then a "trailer" that breaks the scroll and hooks readers before "see more", then closes with a TL;DR and call-to-conversation to drive comments. A typical post of his earns around 230k views and hundreds of comments.

chunks.heading: The three-part structure for a LinkedIn post: meat, trailer, summary
chunks.text:
Justin writes every LinkedIn post in three parts, and builds them in this order:

1. Write "the meat" (the information).
2. Write the "trailer" (the opening that earns the click).
3. Write the summary plus a call-to-conversation (the close).

He says he uses over 10 different processes for writing daily content, but this is the one he shares as a fast, easy way to think about creating it. His context: over 5 years on LinkedIn he generated over 162M impressions (he later updated that to 900M) that power his consulting, product, subscription and sponsorship revenue. Favikon ranked him the #1 global LinkedIn creator 5 times in a row.

chunks.heading: Step one: write the "meat" first
chunks.text:
- The meat is where you teach, show or suggest something. It is the information the reader wants and that you want to convey.
- Justin starts here, before any hook, so the post is anchored in real substance.
- His example post taught readers how he built his online course business. He wrote out 2 learnings and 1 piece of advice he felt were important.
- His caveat: readers may find the suggestions useful, but "they'll never see them if they don't stop to read the content." That is why the trailer comes next.

chunks.heading: Step two: write the "trailer" that breaks the scroll
chunks.text:
The trailer has 2 jobs:
- Break the scroll pattern with the first line.
- Make each line intriguing enough to pull the reader to the next one.

How he builds it, using his example post:
- Line 1 is short and consumable, and uses a big revenue number to stop the scroll. It is built around the $1.5M in course sales.
- Line 2 gives context and signals this is not "some 'get rich quick' post." It is a process that takes time.
- Line 3 is the hook line: _"Here are 2 big learnings and some advice:"_
- He starts by asking what the audience cares about. His audience wants to learn how to produce and sell digital products online, so the first line speaks to that.

chunks.heading: The hook line sits right before "see more"
chunks.text:
- The hook line is the last line visible before LinkedIn's "...see more" button.
- This is where the reader commits to reading on or keeps scrolling.
- Justin says it "absolutely must be intriguing."
- He creates intrigue by promising the reader will learn a few things tied to the $1.5M in course sales.
- If the reader clicks "see more," the trailer has done its job and they move into the meat.

chunks.heading: Step three: close with a TL;DR and a CTC
chunks.text:
- The ending packages the whole post into a few sentences, labeled "TL;DR" (too long, didn't read).
- Purpose: the reader shouldn't have to scroll back up and reread the whole post before joining the comments.
- After the TL;DR he adds a CTC (call-to-conversation), which makes a comment more likely and gives the post more traction.
- Three ways to do a CTC:
  - Ask a question.
  - Ask for a contrarian take.
  - Offer to answer questions.
- The TL;DR plus CTC lets readers review the key points fast and start participating in the comments right away.

chunks.heading: Publishing, results and the three-step checklist
chunks.text:
- Justin schedules the finished post in Taplio, his preferred LinkedIn scheduling tool.
- Result for the example post: 232,471 views, 2,161 interactions and 461 comments. He says this is in line with a typical daily post for him.
- His recap:
  - **Step 1:** Start with the information. What are you teaching or suggesting?
  - **Step 2:** Create the trailer. Does each line get the reader to the next? Is the hook compelling?
  - **Step 3:** Make it easy to engage. Leave a short summary and a CTC.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Justin breaks down the opener of his most successful LinkedIn post (4.766M impressions) into a reusable three-line template. Only 210 characters show above "see more", so the opener works like a thread hook: stop the scroll, flip the script, then add gasoline and a teaser. He turns every post that performs well into a template and reuses it.

chunks.heading: The viral opener template: relatable enemy, hero, gasoline plus teaser
chunks.text:
Justin treats a LinkedIn opener as the whole game. A post has a 3,000-character limit, but only about 210 characters show "above the fold" before the "see more" button. His framing: "You have 210 characters to get people interested in the rest of it." A LinkedIn post works like a Twitter thread, where the first lines decide whether anyone reads the rest.

- Format the opener as 3 short written lines with blank lines between them (3 lines of text, 2 lines of space) so it is easy to read.
- Lines and spacing alone do not make a post viral; the written content does.
- On February 21, 2022 he wrote a post purely to test whether he could produce something viral. He notes his goal is never to go viral, but it was a fun experiment.
- Result: 4.766M impressions, 50,583 engagements, 1,444 comments, 1,589 shares, his most successful LinkedIn post at the time.

chunks.heading: Step 1: The scroll-stopper (relatable enemy plus negativity)
chunks.text:
Justin says the first line "is more important than 95% of the rest of the post. It must be excellent if you want people to read your LinkedIn content."

- Pick a "relatable enemy" the audience already dislikes, then "throw rocks" at it so readers stop scrolling to join in.
- His example: he knew much of his audience dislikes their 9 to 5 jobs, so the enemy was "The 9 to 5".
- Pair the enemy with a negative word so the audience leans in "in glee".
- Formula: "The {RelatableEnemy} is {Negativity}". Example: "The 9 to 5 is getting pummeled."
- Talking negatively about a relatable enemy should draw a positive response from the crowd.

chunks.heading: Step 2: Flip the script (the hero gains ground)
chunks.text:
Once the reader has the positive feeling from line one, he accelerates it by painting life without the enemy.

- Choose the hero, the opposite of the enemy, and say it is gaining ground.
- He compares it to politics: a candidate says the opponent is weakening, then flips to say their own candidacy is gaining ground, which "usually whips the crowd into a frenzy".
- Formula: "The {Hero} is {StrongPositiveStatement}". Example: "The great resignation is growing faster than ever."

chunks.heading: Step 3: Gasoline plus teaser (the click to "see more")
chunks.text:
The last line must take the frenzied reader and hook them into clicking "see more".

- "Pour gasoline on the fire" by saying he loves it: he loves seeing the enemy beaten down and the hero strengthening, as if everyone is crushing the enemy together.
- Then lob a simple teaser question. The "Why?" exists only to get readers past "see more".
- Formula: "And I {gasoline}. {TeaserQuestion}?" Example: "And I love it. Why?"
- The result tarnishes the crowd's enemy, champions the hero, and whips readers into a frenzy.

chunks.heading: The full reusable template
Turn winners into templates
chunks.text: Justin's repeatable process: "For every post that I create that performs well, I analyze the post, turn it into a template, and reuse it multiple times." Instead of chasing new ideas each time, he reverse-engineers what worked in a top performer, extracts the structure into fill-in-the-blank slots, and reuses it.

chunks.heading: LinkedIn versus Twitter writing
chunks.text:
- Twitter content arrives as short tweets of 280 characters or less, easy to skim.
- LinkedIn posts are long-form feed items, so the opener has to earn the click.
- He notes LinkedIn has shifted from a professional "resume" site to a place where creators build 7-figure businesses, and that creators like Sahil Bloom, Nicolas Cole, Dickie Bush and Jack Butcher post there daily.
- Writing on LinkedIn differs from Twitter, and new creators often "hear crickets".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Justin breaks every LinkedIn post into four parts (opener, body, call-to-conversation, image) and tracks a specific metric for each in Taplio. He studies his top 10 posts per metric to find patterns, then re-tests quarterly. He reports a 28.7% quarter-over-quarter engagement lift and follower growth from 586,000 to over 645,000 in 90 days.

chunks.heading: How Justin breaks a LinkedIn post into four testable parts
chunks.text:
Justin treats LinkedIn content as a data problem rather than a guessing game. He started using data on LinkedIn in the summer of 2019, when he was about to quit his job and launch a sales consulting business. He had about 20K followers (building the presence since late 2018), posted about sales a few times a week and got decent engagement. Coming from a sales leadership background, he asked: "What if I bring this approach to LinkedIn?"

- He argues most LinkedIn content is guesswork: people post what they hope gets traction with no data suggesting it will perform. "Guessing is not a strategy."
- He breaks every post into four components: the opener (hook), the body, the call-to-conversation (CTC), and the optional image.
- For each component he tracks a specific metric, which lets him keep improving content quality, engagement and efficiency.
- His analytics tool for this is Taplio. He also uses Short.io to track clicks and click-through rates on posts that contain links.

chunks.heading: Optimizing the opener: sort by impressions
chunks.text:
The opener decides whether a reader clicks "...more" or keeps scrolling, which Justin calls arguably the most important part of the post.

- Method: in Taplio, sort posts by impressions, then look at the top 10 posts and study what the openers have in common.
- Recent finding for his audience: openers made of two short, mobile-optimized lines outperform other styles.
- Caveat: what works for him may not work for others. He says to test different approaches and let the data guide you.

chunks.heading: Optimizing the body: sort by likes
chunks.text:
The body is where the post delivers on the promise made in the opener.

- Method: sort Taplio data by likes. His hypothesis: "If more people like a post, then they likely read it to the end. That means I did something right."
- From the top 10 posts by likes, he studies body length, structure and content type.
- Finding for him: medium-length posts that mix short sentences with bullet points perform best.
- He suggests running the same experiment on your own account to learn what your audience cares about.

chunks.heading: Optimizing the call-to-conversation: sort by engagement percentage
chunks.text:
The call-to-conversation (CTC) is the closing prompt that drives comments.

- Method: sort posts by engagement percentage, meaning what share of the people who saw the post left a comment.
- Finding: specific questions that tap into personal experience get more comments, and more thoughtful ones, than generic questions.
- Example of a strong CTC: "What decision will you make today that your future self will thank you for?" It drew far better responses than the weaker "What's your take on this advice?"

chunks.heading: Optimizing the image: keep it clean
chunks.text:
- He found that Twitter screenshots or Canva images with 1-3 lines of text got higher impressions and engagement rates than posts with more complex graphics or bullet points.
- His rule: keep post images "clean, crisp, and un-busy."

chunks.heading: Results and takeaways
chunks.text:
After a quarter of testing and tracking, Justin had a clear picture of what a high-performing post looks like for his audience at that time.

- Average engagement rate rose 28.7% quarter-over-quarter.
- Followers grew from 586,000 to over 645,000 in 90 days.

His takeaways:

1. Data beats guesswork. Track everything.
2. What works for him may not work for you, so run your own tests.
3. The LinkedIn algorithm evolves. Keep testing and adjust quarterly.
4. Engagement quality matters as much as quantity.

Starting point he recommends: build a simple spreadsheet tracking post performance, test different approaches for each post component, and let the data guide your strategy.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Justin Welsh breaks solo business growth into five phases: stay alive, build systems, growth focused, invest in defense, automate. Each phase calls for different work, and spending limited time on the wrong tasks for your phase is the main risk. Each phase typically takes a year or two, so patience is the differentiator.

chunks.heading: The 5 phases of solopreneurship
chunks.text:
Justin frames a solo business as growing in five phases, each with its own priorities. His point: solopreneurs burn out by "doing the wrong things for the phase your business is in," so the first job is to zoom out and identify your phase.

- Phase 1: Stay Alive
- Phase 2: Build Systems
- Phase 3: Growth Focused
- Phase 4: Invest in Defense
- Phase 5: Automate the Business
- Each phase typically takes a year or two.
- He thinks about his business "in terms of years instead of days." His business moved faster than he expected, and he says yours doesn't have to (or need to).
- The differentiator is patience: "a willingness and determination to outlast most people."
- Planning cadence: long-term goals, yearly strategy, quarterly tactics, daily effort.

chunks.heading: Phase 1: Stay Alive (survive on low cost and free distribution)
chunks.text:
- The start is about survival: keeping the "internet doors open and lights on." Justin argues this is where about 95% of people fail.
- Keep expenses low. Free or cheap website builders and email software are enough. No expensive software, fancy logos or brand systems yet.
- Leverage social media, which is basically free. Use Twitter and especially LinkedIn to share knowledge and expertise. The only investment is time.
- Stay away from ads and expensive marketing campaigns at this stage.

chunks.heading: Phase 2: Build Systems (once you have traction)
chunks.text:
- Trigger: you have some traction, meaning you're making some predictable money.
- A system is a process you can follow to produce a predictable outcome. Examples he lists: idea systems, content systems, email and newsletter systems, customer support systems.
- This is where the structure of the business begins to form.
- Document every task you do repeatedly. Start by outlining the tasks in a document, so when it's time to do or delegate a task you have clear instructions. "No more forgetting how or when to do things."
- His own example: a documented system for writing his newsletter and turning it into 6-12 pieces of short-form social content, stored in his internal business playbook.

chunks.heading: Phase 3: Growth Focused (add weight to the foundation)
chunks.text:
- Strong systems mean the foundation is less likely to crack when you add "additional weight," so this is when to start investing in growth.
- By now you should intimately know your customers and how to acquire more of them.
- Tactics:
  - Expand to another platform if you've been active on only one.
  - Start a newsletter, weekly video series or podcast to reach untapped channels.
  - Pursue strategic partnerships and collaborations with other creators, solopreneurs or business owners to extend reach without significant cost.
- His own path: for the first 2.5 years he created content exclusively on LinkedIn. Then he added Twitter, then the weekly newsletter, and more recently got serious about Instagram.

chunks.heading: Phase 4: Invest in Defense (build a moat against copycats)
chunks.text:
- Success attracts copycats: content stealers, product copiers, and worse. That noise makes it harder to compete in crowded social media.
- Justin says he is currently in phase four. His defensive moves:
  - A professionalized brand system: improving brand systems, messaging and website, aiming to "set the standard for Solopreneur brands."
  - An SEO strategy: a 60-asset SEO campaign to bring more organic traffic to his website.
  - Email automation: he had never used it, and is planning a more customized journey for followers, subscribers and customers.
- The logic: rely less on social media and invest in things that give a "moat."

chunks.heading: Phase 5: Automate the Business (efficiency and predictability)
chunks.text:
- Justin says he hasn't reached this phase, so his thoughts are speculative.
- Paid ads become a fit once systems are in place, branding looks great and landing pages convert at a high level. The goal is spending $1 to generate $2, "basically an automated cash machine."
- Consider a part-time project manager who can:
  - Organize assets: with thousands of social posts, hundreds of newsletters and articles, and many follower questions, have someone organize the archive for easy access.
  - Create a weekly plan: his goal is to own the creative work while a "taskmaster" tells him on Monday morning exactly what to do and why, keeping him on the most important priorities.

chunks.heading: Action step Justin recommends
chunks.text: - Reread the phases, work out where you are, find the relevant suggestions, and choose just one to move forward with next week.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Welsh explains his 1-3-5 content method: create one deep pillar piece, extract three core ideas, and turn each into five micro-pieces. It lets creators produce consistent, varied content across formats without burning out, since results matter more than hours spent.

chunks.heading: The 1-3-5 content method: one pillar piece becomes 16 pieces
chunks.text:
Justin's 1-3-5 method is a repurposing system: create one substantial pillar piece, extract three core ideas, and turn each idea into five micro pieces. The aim is to produce enough content for hungry algorithms without burning out. He has posted on LinkedIn and Twitter every day for five years, and his framing is "Work smarter, not harder", because "we aren't rewarded by the hours we spend, we're rewarded by the results we produce."

- He uses his newsletter as the pillar piece of content.
- He says the idea is adaptable ("the sky's the limit"), so creators should tailor it to their own situation.

chunks.heading: Step 1: Create one pillar piece
chunks.text:
Justin starts with one comprehensive piece that goes deep on a topic relevant to the audience.

- Formats that can serve as the pillar: a long Twitter thread, a detailed blog post or newsletter, or an in-depth YouTube video.
- Pick a topic that addresses a big pain point or question the audience has. His example: "A Step-by-Step Guide to Launching Your First Digital Product."
- He calls this the hardest part of the process, but it makes the rest of the production "much faster and easier" because most of the work is done first.

chunks.heading: Step 2: Extract three core ideas
chunks.text:
From the pillar, he pulls three main concepts or tips. Each should be substantial enough to stand alone as valuable content.

Example from the digital product launch pillar:
1. Validating your product idea
2. Creating a minimum viable product (MVP)
3. Building an effective launch strategy

chunks.heading: Step 3: Turn each core idea into five micro pieces
chunks.text:
For each of the three ideas, he creates five pieces of micro-content:

- Two short written posts, pulling impactful sentences from the pillar content.
- One short-form video summarizing the key point in 60 seconds or less.
- One carousel post breaking the concept down in 5-10 slides.
- One poll or question post: make a statement, then ask a question to engage the audience and gather information.

He says to mix and match based on the kind of content you like producing most.

chunks.heading: The math
chunks.text:
- 1 pillar + (3 ideas x 5 micro pieces) = 16 pieces of content.
- The pieces can be used now and repurposed later.
- He hopes the math motivates creators to spend quality time making the best pillar piece they can, since everything else is derived from it.

chunks.heading: Why the approach works
chunks.text:
- **Consistent messaging:** going deep on a topic and then breaking it into micro-posts means "beating the same drum with some variety," which reinforces brand and message.
- **Meets different consumption preferences:** some people prefer in-depth articles, others prefer quick visuals or short videos. The format spread reaches people where they consume best.
- **Smarter, not just more:** "This method isn't just about creating more content - it's about creating smarter content."
- **Sustainable cadence:** "consistency > perfection." The method lets creators provide value regularly "without running yourself ragged."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Justin lays out a data-driven system for keeping digital product sales going after launch without hard-selling on social. Track hooks, body copy and CTAs to find winning combos, send traffic to relevant articles instead of the homepage, and end each article with a soft CTA to the product.

chunks.heading: The passive-selling model: don't sell on social, sell at the end of articles
chunks.text:
Justin advises creators with big audiences and digital products (a course, recipe books) to stop asking for the sale in social content, because followers get turned off by "selling". His alternative is a micro-funnel:

- Short-form social content builds attention.
- A CTA moves people to the website.
- Articles or newsletter issues end with a "passive" CTA that sells the asset.

He frames the point as working "the numbers": get the product in front of enough interested people without saying "buy this thing". He also argues that after launch, sustained sales are what make a digital asset valuable, and that many entrepreneurs have no longevity strategy. A longevity strategy needs "a process and some data to get better over time", not complexity.

chunks.heading: Three parts of short-form content to track: hook, body, CTA
chunks.text:
Justin treats every social post as three measurable pieces:

- **Hook:** Generally drives about 90% of success in impressions, meaning how many people see the post.
- **Body:** Where you show expertise. It should be helpful enough to show the reader you can solve their problem. He measures it by positive sentiment in the comments.
- **CTA:** Moves people from social content to the website. He measures it by how many people it sends over.

He says to publish enough content to have meaningful metrics on all three. Questions to track constantly:

- Which hooks drive the most impressions?
- Which body copy drives the most positive sentiment?
- Which CTA moves the most people to the website?

chunks.heading: Build "combos" from your top performers
chunks.text:
After 3 to 6 months of publishing, Justin says you should know your top five hooks, body styles and CTAs. Then create "combos": the right hook with the right body and CTA. Using proven combos maximizes impressions and, in turn, website visitors.

His end-state is chain-linked content: best hook, then best body copy, then best CTA, then best "selling" article. He describes this as "maximizing every single piece of your entire micro-funnel."

chunks.heading: Send traffic to relevant articles, not the homepage
chunks.text:
Justin says traffic from social should not go to your homepage. Send it to articles that expand on the specific problem and solution the social post covered. At the end of each article or issue, passively sell your asset, with no hard selling.

Example CTA, for an article on balancing fats, carbs and protein for a leaner body, ending with:

"If you're looking to make this easy, I have a recipe book with 250+ perfectly portioned, simple meals. Get lean, shredded, and healthy with these 30-minute or less recipes in my recipe book here."

He describes this as "Simple. Helpful. Non-aggressive. Really just a 'passive' CTA."

chunks.heading: Test which article sells best
chunks.text:
Justin's process for finding the best "selling" article:

1. Put a passive CTA to your asset at the end of every article.
2. Rotate between about 20 different articles or newsletter issues.
3. Track the conversion rate from article reader to asset buyer.
4. Identify which article is set up to sell best.
5. Create similar articles for other topics.

He calls these articles "24/7/365 salespeople that cost you nothing other than the time it takes to write them", working while you eat, sleep and spend time with family.

chunks.heading: Illustrative math and who it works for
chunks.text:
Justin's example of what a creator with a $30 recipe book might see by doing this effectively:

- 50,000 impressions
- 500 website visitors
- 20 purchases
- $30 per recipe book
- $600 in daily revenue
- $219,000 in yearly revenue

His framing: "Not a bad result for doing the same thing they're already doing." He says it is not just for big creators; anyone with meaningful traction online can do it. The case that prompted the guide involved two entrepreneurs in lower-margin coaching and product businesses, one with a 1M+ LinkedIn/X following and an online course, the other with 1M+ Instagram followers and multiple recipe books. Both were looking for higher-margin, more automated ways to increase profit.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Justin Welsh argues that lead magnets which teach 10% and sell 90% feel like a trick and erode trust. Instead, map your customer's journey, pick an early, narrow step that unlocks the rest, solve it completely for free, and then sell the remainder of the journey.

chunks.heading: Turn the lead magnet into an honest on-ramp: solve one early problem completely
chunks.text:
Justin's complaint about common lead magnets is that they "teach you 10% and then sell you the other 90%." He agrees prospects can tell when information is being held back, and that feeling tricked "erodes any trust you've built." His alternative is a lead magnet that gives away a full solution and still leads naturally to the paid product. He shared this in response to a question from his Creator MBA community.

- The magnet should not look "incomplete on purpose."
- The paid offer picks up where the free one honestly ends.
- Trust is the asset being protected.

chunks.heading: The 'early narrow' problem concept
chunks.text:
Justin's key idea is the "early narrow" problem. It is a crucial early step in the customer's journey that, once solved, unlocks the rest of the "wider journey."

- Solving it fully does not require holding anything back.
- It matters more than a late-stage problem: a mistake at the first step makes the rest "a lot more difficult - probably impossible," while a mistake at the last step is minor (his example: a pizza that is "a bit too burned").
- Problems of this type "make wonderful lead magnets."

chunks.heading: Step 1 and 2: map the journey, then pick the early narrow step
chunks.text:
Justin's process starts with the customer's overall journey, the one your paid products and services help with.

1. List everything the ideal customer needs to figure out to reach their big goal.
2. Order the list into the most logical sequence.
3. Pick the early narrow problem from that sequence.

His worked example is someone teaching home pizza-making through courses and cookbooks. The steps are: make good dough, roll it out well, choose the sauce, choose the amount of toppings, heat the pizza oven correctly, get the pizza onto the peel correctly, rotate it correctly, and get time, temperature and doneness right. Dough is the early narrow problem. He notes the steps are "easy to read and VERY hard to do," and says he messed up his first ten pizzas himself.

chunks.heading: Step 3: solve it completely, then sell the rest
chunks.text:
The lead magnet should fully solve the narrow problem. In the pizza example, it teaches excellent dough for a home pizza oven, start to finish. Justin lists two results of this approach:

- **No one is tricked.** The magnet promised to solve the dough problem and delivered.
- **The rest of the journey is unlocked.** The customer can do the first critical step successfully and carry on. You become "a trusted guide early in their journey," which makes you the logical choice to keep working with.

At the end of the magnet, mention the remaining problems and position the paid course or cookbooks as the solution to them. His sample close: "Now that you have the perfect pizza dough, you're ready to join 1,000+ other students in transforming your dough into world-class home pizza. If you found my dough lesson helpful, consider joining my course today where you'll learn the secrets to rolling your dough, choosing the correct toppings, and a complete masterclass on using your pizza oven..."

chunks.heading: The lead magnet recipe (summary checklist)
chunks.text:
1. Write down all the steps prospects must take to reach their ultimate outcome.
2. Arrange the steps into a logical sequence.
3. Identify an "early narrow" problem: a crucial early step that, when solved, unlocks the rest of the journey.
4. Design a lead magnet that "100% solves that narrow problem" and give it all away generously.
5. Sell the remainder of the journey in a simple video, an email series, or inside the lead magnet itself.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Justin Welsh explains "digital leverage" as using the internet to get more output with less time and effort. The system has three stages: turn one idea into one long-form piece and about 10 social posts, use those posts to passively sell, then compound sales with a generous affiliate program.

chunks.heading: Digital leverage: the three-part formula
chunks.text:
Justin defines "Digital Leverage" as using the internet to achieve more with less time, effort and resources. He treats it as essential for a one-person business, where there are only 24 hours in a day.

- He frames it as the difference between mastering your work and your work mastering you.
- He rejects "Hustle 24/7" culture: "The biggest flaw of the 24/7 hustle culture is the misconception that if you work hard enough, you will succeed in the end. You win with leverage. Not brute force."
- The formula has three parts:
  - **Content:** Think 1x, Publish 10x
  - **Selling:** Publish 10x, Sell 100x
  - **Compounding:** Sell 100x, Compound 1,000x
- Weekly action step: find one spot in your online presence or business where digital leverage could help, and commit to trying it for 30 days.

chunks.heading: Think 1x, Publish 10x: one idea becomes many pieces
chunks.text:
Justin's best content starts with a single idea, then gets multiplied.

- **Finding the idea:** with his audience in mind, he researches trending topics, reads industry insights, and engages on social media for an hour every day.
- **Creating the core piece:** after choosing a topic, he writes one robust long-form piece. It might be a newsletter issue, an article or a Twitter thread. The goal is for it to be packed with value for the target audience.
- **Breaking it up:** he splits the long piece into smaller, more digestible pieces such as tweets, LinkedIn posts, Twitter threads and Instagram posts. One big idea becomes about 10 small pieces.
- He points to his Content OS as the system he uses for this repurposing.

chunks.heading: Publish 10x, Sell 100x: distribution as passive selling
chunks.text:
Once he has about 10 small pieces from one idea, he publishes them in every place that makes sense for each piece (Twitter, LinkedIn, Instagram and so on).

- **Why it sells:** more high-value touch points across platforms means more chances to engage the audience, build trust, and position yourself as an expert and authority.
- **Trust drives purchases:** the more your audience values your free content, the more likely they are to invest in your paid offerings.
- **Repurposing reaches more people:** turning one strong piece into bite-sized posts for different platforms reaches a wider audience with minimal effort.
- **The "trojan horse" tactic:** use the free social posts to promote products and services. Simple ways include:
  - linking back to your website
  - promoting a testimonial
  - encouraging people to read an article or blog post that links to your products or services
- He calls this "passive selling" and says it works much better, in his opinion, than aggressively promoting yourself all the time.

chunks.heading: Sell 100x, Compound 1,000x: affiliate programs
chunks.text:
Justin treats 100 sales as more than a milestone. He sees it as the chance to compound sales through incentives.

- **The idea:** incentivize happy customers to spread the word. With 100 customers, you have a small army who can send you more customers.
- **The math:** if each of 100 original customers brings in 10 new customers, that is 1,000 additional sales.
- **Why referrals work:** potential customers trust a recommendation from someone they know more than any landing page or website.
- **The mechanism:** an affiliate program where customers earn a commission on every new customer they refer.
- **His commission rate:** he pays 35% rather than the standard 20%, because he wants people to "feel empowered to earn."

chunks.heading: Three requirements for a win-win-win affiliate program
chunks.text:
Justin says an affiliate program needs three things:

1. **A high-quality product or service.** People only refer friends if they truly got value from the offering.
2. **A good enough incentive.** You can't pay out pennies and expect people to keep the program top of mind.
3. **Transparency.** Explain how the program works, when people get paid, and give helpful tips for promoting or talking about the products.

His summary: get content, selling and compounding right, and you see more happy customers, more revenue and better efficiency, using internet tools strategically to keep the business moving without constant brute force.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Justin Welsh lays out 7 steps he'd follow to start an online business from zero: pick one problem for one specific group, package a clear roadmap, ship a simple $50-$150 product fast, find customers on a few channels, collect testimonials, and build a repeatable selling system backed by simple daily-sales math.

chunks.heading: The core thesis: one problem, one audience, one roadmap
chunks.text:
Justin argues that most first online businesses fail because of a stack of wrong choices: niche, messaging, ideal customer, pricing structure, product offering. His fix is narrowness at the start.

- Pick one problem that one very specific group of people share. Not "all problems" or "all people."
- Find it by looking backward: a problem he solved for himself a few years ago.
- Example: you and your friends at a local state college all wanted a job at a great tech company, but only you figured out how. That is a solution to a common problem.

chunks.heading: Package the solution as a roadmap (Point A to Point B)
chunks.text:
- "We overestimate how much people want to learn at once." Most people want to solve one problem: get from point A to point B "easily, quickly, and affordably."
- Craft the offer as a roadmap or blueprint aimed at a specific audience.
- Example offer: "The 14-day roadmap that shows state college graduates how to land their dream job at Google."

chunks.heading: Product format and hosting: pick something simple and finish it
chunks.text:
- Format matters much less than the problem and the roadmap. Pick whatever you are likely to complete: writers make an eBook, teachers record a video course, systems people build digital materials.
- Uses Parkinson's Law ("work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion") to justify timeboxing. Set a specific deadline; he suggests starting with something fast, like 28 days.
- For hosting, don't overcomplicate it. He recommends Stan Store or something similarly simple. "Get complicated down the road. Just make sales now."

chunks.heading: Pricing: $50 to $150 for a first product
chunks.text:
- Charge between $50 and $150. That is affordable enough to get buyers without needing years of built trust.
- The goal is to deliver thousands of dollars' worth of value, if not more, relative to the price.

chunks.heading: Finding the first customers: test channels, then triple down
chunks.text:
- Justin says the best place to find customers is LinkedIn.
- Other channels he lists: articles on Medium or your own site, Twitter, Twitter snapshots reposted on Instagram, Quora answers, IndieHackers and Makerpad posts, subreddits, and Facebook groups.
- It is work, but it teaches you which distribution channels lead to sales. "You want to find which of these channels leads to sales and then triple down."

chunks.heading: Social proof: turn customers into testimonials
chunks.text:
- Once you have a few customers, automate testimonial collection. He uses Testimonial.to, triggered at the midway point and end of each of his courses.
- Display testimonials everywhere: website, landing page, social media, articles, blogs.
- "Social proof sells." His course pages are deliberately heavy with it.
- Result he cites for The Operating System page: 4.7% of visitors buy, leading to roughly $130k+ in sales every 30 days for that product.

chunks.heading: A repeatable selling system and the math behind a 6-figure product
chunks.text:
- Every good online business has a repeatable system: know exactly where you post each day, at what time, and why.
- Track separately which content drives impressions and engagement versus which drives visits and purchases ("They are different"). Intersperse both types: attention content, then conversion content.
- Target: find 4 people per day who will buy a $75 course. 4 x $75 x 365 = $109,500, a 6-figure product.
- Work backward from the target. With a 3.5% site conversion rate, you need to drive about 114 people to your site daily. Find your best channel and get 114 people there with something that piques their interest.
- He frames the path as requiring "a long-term growth mindset, patience, and an engaged audience on a social platform of your choice."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Justin Welsh lays out a four-step growth plan for building an audience from zero: pick a tight niche, hold a non-obvious point of view, tell a real backstory, and do unscalable work early. He backs it with his own routine of daily posting, replying to every comment and DM, and hundreds of Zoom calls with followers.

chunks.heading: Pick a narrow audience before you create anything
chunks.text:
- Justin cites streaming: in 2021 Netflix and Hulu fell from 65% to 48% market share, while niche streaming services grew at more than 2x the rate of the majors. His reading: "niche content resonates."
- He tells creators to build their own niche "streaming service" for the right audience.
- Target a specific person with a specific problem. "Help small businesses" is too vague. "SaaS companies in the finance vertical, below $10M in revenue" is the level of specificity he recommends.
- The tighter the audience, the more likely they are to find your "signal" in a world of generic "noise."
- He says most creators fail because they have no plan. They post daily, get no traction, and quit. He calls a growth plan the actual "how" behind an audience goal, and it replaces random content and products nobody buys.

chunks.heading: Stand out with non-obvious content (Category Pirate)
chunks.text:
- A niche gets you a small group of followers. Over time, sharing only obvious tactics people can learn anywhere makes meaningful content harder to produce.
- His fix is non-obvious content: a brand-new thought process for your niche that makes you radically different from others.
- He endorses Nicolas Cole's "Category Pirates" idea. Cole's point, which Justin quotes: you don't need everyone to care, "just a small pirate ship of folks who agree with your unique perspective," and that is enough to get paid to do what you love.
- Warning: "if you just say what other people are saying, you become a commodity."
