- He credits interesting, unique, non-obvious things to say for growing past 600,000 LinkedIn followers, which he calls the easiest place to build a brand.
- Questions he asks to find your viewpoint:
  - What does everyone believe that you don't?
  - What is nobody in your niche talking about that they should be?
  - What are the biggest mistakes people make without realizing it?
  - Why are you worth following when others aren't?

chunks.heading: Tell a real backstory people can see themselves in
chunks.text:
- A resonant backstory, he says, is gasoline on the fire once you have a niche and a unique perspective.
- He calls this building a better backstory. Like a startup founder, you need a story that compels people to follow you, and they must "literally see themselves in you."
- It can't be made up or fake. It should be your real story, stitched together so it is easy and exciting to follow.
- He has a 7-step process for doing this and published it as a free guide ("Build a Better Backstory").

chunks.heading: Do unscalable things early
chunks.text:
- Justin says the idea of putting this on autopilot early is "couldn't be further from the truth." In the beginning you must do things that don't scale.
- His own early list:
  1. Published daily to social media, often 2-3 times per day.
  2. Replied to every comment, every morning, for over an hour.
  3. Responded to 85%+ of the DMs he got on LinkedIn and Twitter.
  4. Commented on 10-15 people's content every morning for over a year.
  5. Attended over 300 Zoom meetings with followers in his first 2 years.
- He ties these activities to growth past 600,000 followers on LinkedIn and 495,000 on X/Twitter.
- He says he cannot overstate how important it is to be everywhere when you start. Many people call this "creating value," and he argues it needs a deeper definition, endorsing Daniel Vassallo's take on it (the quote itself is not included in the source).

chunks.heading: The 4-step plan to 1,000 true fans
chunks.text:
1. Think like a niche streaming service: a specific audience with a specific need.
2. Become a Category Pirate: a unique, non-obvious perspective inside that niche.
3. Tell a story worth following: a real backstory your audience sees themselves in.
4. Do unscalable things: daily posting, replying, DMs, commenting, and calls with followers.

His claim: nail these four and "you are absolutely on your way to 1,000 true fans."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Justin shares his Friday ritual for planning the week ahead using eight questions. The process eliminates, automates and delegates low-value work, protects time for creative work, family and fun, and keeps a one-person business aligned with his values and goals.

chunks.heading: The weekly preview ritual
chunks.text:
Every Friday, Justin runs a "weekly preview": a short review of the coming week's calendar built around eight questions. It is not a to-do list or a calendar glance. The goal is a schedule that "supports what's truly important: my life."

- He pitches it for anyone "flying by the seat of your pants" or jumping on back-to-back calls with no room for creative work.
- He says to steal, adapt or drop questions; not all eight are needed.
- The point is to "have a process to ensure that your life isn't flying by without stopping to think about whether you're truly living."
- He frames it as aligning the calendar with his values, goals and the realities of a one-person business.

chunks.heading: Remove, automate, delegate
chunks.text:
The first three questions cut the workload before anything else is scheduled.

- **What can I remove?** Schedules fill up with commitments that don't serve bigger goals. "Elimination is your best friend as a Solopreneur or Creator." Look ahead and cut time spent on things that don't support goals.
- **What can be automated?** Each week he looks for tasks to automate to free up time and mental energy.
- **What should be delegated but isn't?** Delegate tasks that cost more time than they're worth.

chunks.heading: Automation example: newsletter sponsorships
chunks.text:
Sponsorships were once a clunky manual process: a form to fill out, then long email back-and-forth with the sponsor. Now the flow is:

Buy button → Submission of Copy → Calendar Invite → Newsletter Publication

- This saves him about 30 minutes a week.
- It is also a simple experience for the sponsor.
- The newsletter reaches 200,000+ entrepreneurs (per the essay's sponsor call-to-action).

chunks.heading: Delegation example: customer service
chunks.text:
- He used to spend 45 minutes every single day on customer service tickets: invoices, login questions, "can't find something."
- He outsourced it to his virtual assistant, who handles every issue that hits her inbox. She has the time and focus to keep customers happy, and he no longer thinks about it.
- His regret: "I waited far too long to delegate anything. And I wish I hired her sooner."

chunks.heading: Protecting urgent and important work: urgency, meeting length
chunks.text:
- **Urgent vs. important:** "We often mistake urgent for important." He scrutinizes the calendar for what is genuinely critical right now. A meeting that isn't important at this moment gets pushed 60-90 days out, making space for things that are urgent AND important.
- **Shorter meetings:** "Most meetings can be halved in length without losing substance or outcomes." The question he asks is whether any important meeting can be 50% shorter.
- If a meeting has no agenda, ask for one; the meeting can then likely shrink significantly.
- For podcasts, he tells hosts he can't do 60 or 90 minutes and that 45 minutes is his max. As a host, he applies the same principle.

chunks.heading: Life-side questions: screen time and fun
chunks.text:
- **Get off the computer more:** He doesn't want his life lived in front of a screen, which is a daily challenge for someone who earns a living online. He prioritizes stepping away, engaging with the world and nourishing creativity offline.
- He built systems for creating Twitter and newsletter content (Content OS) and for growing quickly on LinkedIn (The Operating System) without spending exorbitant time online.
- **Maximize fun time:** Family time is "paramount," and it is easy to overlook in solopreneurship, so he carves it out deliberately.
- Each week he prioritizes trips, dinners, mid-week lunches, comedy shows and time with friends.
- His claim: he needs fun to keep creative juices flowing, and "the more fun I have with family and friends, the more creative ideas I get."

chunks.heading: Final check: is anything missing?
chunks.text:
- After the first seven questions, he reflects on the new-look week, watching for gaps or opportunities missed on the first pass.
- It is a chance to confirm "with 100% certainty" that the schedule aligns with his values and immediate goals.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Justin lays out what he'd do if starting over today: pick a niche at the intersection of skill, passion and willingness to pay, post with a "Teach, Teach, Teach, Sell" mix, comment on 9 relevant posts daily, and use analytics to adjust. Built for LinkedIn but works on other platforms.

chunks.heading: Starting from zero: a four-step LinkedIn plan to build a niche brand
chunks.text: Justin divides his career into three phases: years of failures and setbacks, a turnaround after finding passion at work, and then applying those lessons to his first business. In May 2024 he wrote that if he were starting over today, he would run a simple four-step plan to focus on what he loves, get attention, build a following, and position himself to land business. He built it for LinkedIn because he thinks it is "the easiest place to grow a brand and business right now," but says it could be executed on another social platform.

chunks.heading: Step 1: Find the niche at the intersection of skill, love and willingness to pay
chunks.text:
- Start by identifying the intersection of three things: something you're good at, something you love to do, and something people are willing to pay you for.
- His own starting niche was teaching founders how to build sales teams to sell their software to physicians. He notes this is very different from what he teaches now, but it is how he started as an entrepreneur.
- Sharpen the niche by adding a unique angle. His example: someone passionate about public speaking who is also an introvert could position as "Confident Public Speaking for Introverted Professionals."
- The test is whether people with that specific profile would pay to become as good a speaker as you are.

chunks.heading: Step 2: The "Teach, Teach, Teach, Sell" content framework
chunks.text:
- In the beginning, you need to make people aware you exist. He calls LinkedIn the dominant platform for getting attention right now.
- The framework balances content: about 80% of the time you provide value to the audience, and about 20% of the time you softly promote your expertise, products or services.
- It runs as a 5-post cycle: three teaching posts (he later lists four in his example), then a soft sell. His public speaking example:
  - Post 1 (Teach): a step-by-step guide to structuring a compelling presentation.
  - Post 2 (Teach): the top 5 breathing exercises to calm nerves before a presentation.
  - Post 3 (Teach): a framework introverts can use to remember their speech on stage.
  - Post 4 (Teach): a guide to handling audience Q&A at the end of a speech.
  - Post 5 (Sell): a soft pitch for coaching services, stressing the unique approach for introverted professionals, ideally weaving in your story.
- Followed consistently, this builds the "trust, expertise, and authority" he says you need in a niche to generate leads for a coaching business.

chunks.heading: Step 3: Engage daily with the "$0.18 Strategy"
chunks.text:
- The original is Gary Vaynerchuk's "$1.80 Strategy": leave your "two cents" on 9 relevant posts across 10 hashtags every day ($0.02 x 9 posts x 10 hashtags = $1.80).
- Justin calls that overkill. He used a simpler version when starting on LinkedIn, the "$0.18 strategy": leave your two cents on 9 relevant posts per day. He says to adapt it as you wish.
- Benefits: more visibility, new and relevant connections, and making your name, face and brand "a regularly occurring character on the platform."
- How to do it:
  1. Find 9 posts (or 9 people) in your LinkedIn feed relevant to your niche.
  2. Leave a thoughtful comment on each. Avoid "good post" or "agree." Share insights and experiences, tell stories, add knowledge that expands the post, or ask a good question to drive discussion.
  3. Repeat daily for a year to build relationships and visibility.
- The more your comment is the most relevant one, the more people see your name and face, "and that's how a following gets built."

chunks.heading: Step 4: Track results and adjust
chunks.text:
- "None of this stuff matters if you're not tracking what's working and what isn't."
- Use LinkedIn Analytics or Shield to track post performance and overall presence.
- Look for which content types, subjects, styles, structures, days or times generate the most engagement, and adjust.
- Pay attention to the demographics of people interacting with the content and tailor content to their interests and needs. If you don't know what people want, ask them.
- Keep refining based on data and follower feedback.

chunks.heading: Principles behind the plan
chunks.text:
- No strategy is perfect and there are a million ways to start building a brand, but following these four steps while "stay[ing] committed to helping your target audience" should create traction on LinkedIn and a serious presence in a niche.
- Order matters: pick the niche first, then teach consistently, engage with the audience daily, and let analytics steer.
- He references a free 20-step guide covering his advice after growing his business from $0 to $7.5M in 4 years and 8 months, which he says is an evolving document.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Justin argues attention is three things working together, not just a great hook. After 4,000+ pieces of content, he found you need a pattern disruption, a relevance snap (this is about me), and emotional accuracy (specific, real moments over stats). Miss one and you are noise in the feed.

chunks.heading: Attention is three things at once: pattern disruption, relevance snap, emotional accuracy
chunks.text:
Justin argues that attention in 2025 is a bigger battle than before. People have trained their brains to ignore almost everything. "Scroll, skim, and forget" is how they consume, and with 10,000+ posts a day the brain builds an automatic filter. He says most creators are now fighting that reflex, not specific competitors.

- He used to think attention came from "hooks," then "providing value," "being consistent," and authenticity.
- After 6 years and 4,000+ unique pieces of content, he concluded that attention "isn't one thing." It is three things working together.
- If you miss any one, "you're just more noise in someone's feed." Nail all three and "they can't help but pay attention."

chunks.heading: The 2019 post that taught him the formula
chunks.text:
Justin reread a 2019 LinkedIn post that opened like a hustle-and-grind morning routine post.

- Readers stopped after the opening and got furious. Comments included "Another bro-ey morning routine!", "Another productivity hack!" and "Another guy trying to make me feel lazy!"
- The post flipped completely in the second half. Readers who reached the end reacted differently: they left reactions, dropped nice comments, and 206 people shared it with friends.
- People went from hate-reading to saving and reposting.
- Lesson: the opening grabbed attention through an immediate emotional response, and the payoff turned that attention into engagement and shares.

chunks.heading: Part 1: Pattern disruption
chunks.text:
Pattern disruption is "something that makes a person's brain stutter." It breaks the mental autopilot that filters out feed content.

- In the 2019 post, the first lines worked because they triggered an instant emotional reaction. Readers assumed it was a hustle post and leaned in angrily.
- He says pattern disruption alone is not enough to earn attention that lasts.
- Hypothetical example he gives of a disruptive opener: "I haven't had coffee in 97 days."

chunks.heading: Part 2: The relevance snap
chunks.text:
The relevance snap is the moment a reader thinks, "Wait...this is about me." The content shifts from a general topic to the reader's specific experience.

- In the 2019 post, he moved from "hustling entrepreneurs" and "creators trying to make it happen" to something broader: "anyone who's ever felt like they're falling short of their own impossible standards." He notes that describes most people.
- Broad audience labels don't create the snap. Naming a feeling the reader recognizes does.
- Hypothetical example: a specific scene like "that 2:30 PM meeting where everyone else is caffeinated and you're running on willpower."

chunks.heading: Part 3: Emotional accuracy
chunks.text:
Justin says this is "where most creators fail." They write to sound smart when they should write to make people feel seen.

- Bad (data-driven, generic, boring): "Studies show that 87% of professionals struggle with maintaining consistent morning routines."
- Good (specific, vulnerable, real): "Most days I wake up at 6 a.m., scramble to get through my Duolingo while brushing my teeth."
- He says stats make him yawn. They may be true, but they make people nod and keep scrolling.
- The good line is "the sound of someone's actual morning," so readers think "holy shit, that's literally me right now."
- Summary: "The bad example tries to prove a point, while the good example shares a real moment."
- Hypothetical example: naming an emotion others feel but can't articulate, such as "the weird pride of being the only person who doesn't need stimulants to function."

chunks.heading: Clickbait is only clickbait if you don't deliver
chunks.text:
Justin says "Something isn't clickbait if you deliver," especially if you take the audience on a journey where they discover something extremely useful.

- This freed him to write content that felt "wrong" or highly polarizing, and to open with pattern disruption, because if someone pauses he can deliver something worth their time.
- Each part of a post has a job:
  - Opening: breaks their mental pattern.
  - Body: makes them see themselves in your words.
  - Payoff: gives them something they'll remember and save.
- Common failure modes, where creators get only one part right:
  - Great hooks, but no emotional appeal.
  - Helpful content, but writing so boring nobody stops to read it.
  - Strong emotion, but not useful enough to apply or share with friends.
- "The good stuff happens when you start mixing all three together successfully."

chunks.heading: Diagnosing why some posts get ignored and others don't
chunks.text:
Justin says creators often post "into the void" while someone's random coffee thought gets 10,000 likes. His view is that the difference isn't the idea but "how the idea is executed."

- Diagnostic: a post that stops you almost certainly does all three (pattern break, relevance snap, emotional accuracy). A post you scroll past is missing at least one.
- For years he chased individual tactics: better hooks, stronger CTAs, more consistency, more value. His conclusion is that attention in 2025 requires "engineering the complete experience."
- The sequence runs from the brain stuttering on the opening, to engaging because the reader sees themselves in it, to sharing because it is genuinely useful.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Justin argues that too many offers and price tiers cause decision fatigue and quietly kill sales. He recommends one course, one community and one service, each with a single price, so customers only choose how they want to "do it": alone, with others, or done for them.

chunks.heading: Offer count and decision fatigue
chunks.text:
Justin argues that too many offers lower sales through "decision fatigue": too many options wear out the buyer's brain and make a choice harder. His example is a Creator MBA Office Hours student with four service offerings, five digital courses at multiple price points and three community membership tiers. That business made a few thousand dollars a month. The student's reason was "I want to give people choices."

- Each added option is another decision point. It adds time and questions before the customer can move forward.
- "At some point, people would rather make no decision than the wrong decision."
- Analogies: an old-school diner with a 100+ item menu versus an eight-item menu (fewer choices means a faster decision), and spending 30 minutes scrolling Netflix and watching nothing.
- His question to ask of your own offers: "Are you really serving your audience by giving them more choices? Or are you just making it harder for them to say yes?"

chunks.heading: Why tiered courses stall buyers
chunks.text:
Justin's example is a beginner course, an intermediate course, an advanced course and a bundle of all three. It looks logical, but the buyer starts thinking: "Should I start with beginner? What if it's too basic? Maybe I should get the bundle...but that's a bigger investment...which one is right for me?"

- The buyer does "mental gymnastics" and ends up choosing nothing.
- His own practice: each course he offers has one price, "That's it."
- The fix for courses: if you're just starting out, one course at one price is enough.

chunks.heading: Why tiered service packages stall buyers
chunks.text:
Justin's example is three service tiers, such as $497, $997 and $2,997, each with a slightly different scope of work.

- The prospect compares packages and works out what they really need. They also wonder whether the extra $500 is worth it, or whether they could get some of the top option's work in the middle one. They probably choose nothing.
- His own practice when he offered consulting: one offer tailored to the most common needs of his clients, "Take it or leave it."
- The fix for services: a core service offering, with (maybe) an accelerated offer to get results faster.

chunks.heading: Recommended offer set: one course, one community, one service
chunks.text:
Justin's guidance for cutting offers down:

- **Courses:** one course with one price when starting out.
- **Community:** at most two membership types, community and private mastermind.
- **Services:** a core offering, maybe plus an accelerated version.
- "Most of the time, one course, one community, and one service is perfect."

chunks.heading: Using the three offers as a natural value ladder
chunks.text:
With one of each product type, Justin says you create a natural value ladder that matches how customers want to reach their intended outcome. The customer's choice becomes only how they want to "do it":

- **Course:** "I'm going to buy the course and do this on my own."
- **Community:** "I'm going to join the community and do this with other people."
- **Service:** "I'm going to hire you 1:1 and have you do it for me."

He frames this as the better way to give people options: choice between modes of doing it (alone, with others, done for you), not between near-duplicate products and price points.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: When Twitter's algorithm change capped his daily newsletter signups at about 250, Welsh ran an experiment: the 1-Tweet CTA vs. the 2-Tweet CTA. He moved the link into a second Tweet so the first could reach people without a link. The lesson is to keep testing as algorithms shift.

chunks.heading: Why Justin tests social media tactics constantly
chunks.text:
- Justin treats social media as an experimentation lab. He is "always testing and measuring and modifying" his strategies.
- He credits a big part of his social success to trying new things to learn what works and what doesn't.
- His rule: social media algorithms are always on the move, and "as content creators, it's our job to adapt and experiment."
- He applies the same experimentation mindset to "everything else in your business."

chunks.heading: The 2022 Twitter-to-newsletter formula and why it stopped working
chunks.text:
- Through 2022, Justin used Twitter to drive traffic to his website, with the goal of attracting newsletter subscribers.
- A November 2022 Tweet shows the formula. Engagement was low (158 vs. an average of 800+), yet it still produced 593 new subscribers.
- Takeaway: the Tweet's job was subscriber conversion, not engagement. He judged it on subscribers, not likes.
- Early in 2023, Twitter's algorithm changed and the formula stopped delivering. He couldn't get past 250 new subscribers on any given day, a sharp drop from a month earlier.
- He chose not to wait for things to "go back to normal." He wanted to recapture the old subscriber count and keep growing the newsletter, so he ran an experiment.

chunks.heading: The 1-Tweet CTA vs. 2-Tweet CTA experiment
chunks.text:
- Justin named the test the "1-Tweet CTA vs. the 2-Tweet CTA."
- Hypothesis: the LinkedIn algorithm is known to dislike posts with links, and he suspected the new Twitter algorithm disliked Tweets with links too.
- Change: he moved the CTA (the link) out of the main Tweet and into a second Tweet, making a tiny thread of two short Tweets.
- Control: the original format put the link in the single Tweet.

chunks.heading: Results of the 2-Tweet CTA
chunks.text:
- Tweet 1 had no CTA and generated 802K impressions.
- Tweet 2 had the CTA link and generated 39K impressions.
- The thread produced 870 new email subscribers, versus the roughly 250-per-day ceiling he'd been stuck at under the 1-Tweet format.
- The headline claim of the essay (the "4x conversion") rests on this comparison of the post-algorithm-change ceiling against this result.
- He kept using the trick afterward "because it seems to appease the new Twitter algorithm. For now, at least."

chunks.heading: Reusable playbook: keep the link out of the post that needs reach
chunks.text:
- Put the hook or valuable content in the first post with no link, so the algorithm distributes it widely.
- Put the CTA link in a second post or reply. Only a fraction of viewers see it (39K of 802K impressions here), but it was enough to convert at scale.
- Justin says the same approach works for any CTA: newsletter subscribers, product purchases, "or whatever CTA you're after."
- Treat the tactic as temporary. Re-test when the algorithm shifts, since it is only known to work "for now."

Stack rank them from most likely to least likely to be the culprit. Start by cutting everything except the top 2 or 3.

4. Prove or disprove

Don't guide the data. Let the data guide you. Were you right? Wrong? Talk to people as well. Qualitative and quantitative feedback are useful.

5. Install

Once you've figured out the actual fix, install it. Then move on to the next problem.
